articles.title: New US sanctions put pressure on Iran as petrol queues form
articles.body:
Washington has turned to pulling economic levers six months into a war on Iran that has ground to a stalemate militarily, with peace talks stalled and most traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz blocked.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, saying the "objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime".
Announcing the new sanctions, Bessent said countries that did not support the US economic campaign would "share in the isolation" of Iran, adding Trump was making phone calls to world leaders asking that they halt interactions with Tehran.
The Treasury Department said expanded secondary sanctions would target Iran's digital assets and its technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors.
It also issued new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels that allegedly aid Iran in oil revenue generation, weapons procurement and cyber operations.
Iran, however, was dismissive of the threat and predicted "another defeat" for Washington.
"We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," said Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh.
Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs, Kazem Gharibabadi, told Iranian television that Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz “has put great pressure on the American side”, adding that developments on Tuesday were largely in line with demands Tehran had made before negotiations.
Gharibabadi said the current developments could be interpreted as a “retreat” by the US administration from its previous positions.
Explaining the details of the Iranian-Omani understanding on the Strait of Hormuz, he stressed that the agreement did not mean the strait would reopen immediately, saying the two issues were separate.
Gharibabadi said ships had travelled through Omani waters for the past 58 years, causing “serious damage to Iran”. He added that the Strait of Hormuz had now become an issue of Iranian national security, requiring fundamental changes to maritime entry and exit routes.
Under the understanding, vessels entering the Gulf would travel through Iranian waters, while those leaving would use Omani territorial waters, with ships on both routes passing through Iranian waters.
The deputy foreign minister described the arrangement as being “like a highway back and forth”, with a total width of around seven miles.
He said the route was temporary and that Iran and Oman would need to negotiate a new permanent route within 30 to 60 days to replace the previous maritime traffic arrangement.
US envoy hails dissolution of Kurdish-led force in Syria
The United States on Tuesday hailed the dissolution of a Kurdish-led, Washington-backed force in Syria that was at the forefront of the battle against the Islamic State group, and its merger into the country's army.
"This is what real integration looks like: not winners and losers, but former counterparts with differing points of view crafting a diplomatic solution to strengthen the sovereign nation of Syria. One army, one government, one state," said the US special envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, who is also the ambassador to Turkey.
Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday attacked journalists from news agency AFP reporting on tension with Palestinians, in violence that left at least five people injured, the reporters and medics said.
A three-person team from the international news agency had travelled to the village of Jannatah near Bethlehem to report on Israeli activists who conduct solidarity visits to support Palestinians facing harassment by Israeli settlers, who recently blocked a road in the area.
After an altercation broke out between the settlers and activists, the Israeli military ordered journalists to leave what it called a "closed military zone", at which point two additional cars full of settlers swooped in.
The settlers, many of them children, threw stones towards the journalists and activists. According to AFP, one journalist ducked a stone but then a child settler struck him in the chin with a stick, causing minor bleeding, he said.
AFP added that the journalists returned to see their two parked cars both damaged, with back windshields smashed in and tyres punctured. Activists' cars suffered similar damage.
Five people were treated for injuries, the Palestine Red Crescent Society said, with AFP journalists reporting seeing at least one Israeli activist taken in a Palestinian ambulance.
During the clash an Israeli soldier temporarily seized the camera of a video journalist but handed it back afterward, the AFP journalists reported.
An Israeli military spokesperson said that the temporary confiscation of the camera "is currently being reviewed".
Israeli police joined the military to collect evidence on the damage to cars and "a police investigation has been opened into the incident", the military spokesperson said.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, home to around three million Palestinians, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government advancing more construction ahead of October 27 elections.
Violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers has increased dramatically since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas from the Gaza Strip.
Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs, Kazem Gharibabadi, has warned that US mine-detection vessels would become “very good targets” for Iran if they entered the region.
He said US President Donald Trump’s statements on demining were “only aimed at calming the markets”.
Gharibabadi said Tehran’s response to US sanctions would shift towards targeting what he described as the economic interests of its adversaries, rather than responding to the measures through previous methods.
He also questioned why Iran should wait for the United States to launch an attack, raising the possibility that Tehran could take pre-emptive action.
Gharibabadi said Iran would unveil new capabilities if US measures continued.
He added that the Strait of Hormuz was not Iran’s only means of responding to the United States, warning that Washington should not assume it was the only side capable of causing economic damage.
Britain backs US efforts for diplomatic solution on Iran
British Finance Minister John Healey said on Tuesday that the country supports U.S. efforts to secure a diplomatic solution on Iran and welcomed steps to increase pressure, including the expanded sanctions on Iran announced Monday.
Healey also called on Iran to cease its "de-stabilising activity" across the region, including in the Strait of Hormuz.
Israel expels Dutch officials over ‘anti-Israel moves’
Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has announced the immediate expulsion of Dutch representatives from the International Support Center for Gaza in Israel, citing what he described as “a series of anti-Israel moves by the Dutch government”.
“I decided so today, with the approval of Prime Minister Netanyahu,” Sa’ar said, pointing to a Dutch law banning trade in Israeli products from the occupied West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, which is set to come into force next month.
Sa’ar said the Dutch embassy in Israel and US officials were notified on Sunday evening, with the representatives given one week to leave the country.
He claimed the Dutch government’s policies had been “accompanied by an unprecedented wave of antisemitism and boycotts” in the Netherlands.
“Whoever acts against Israel will have no foothold in the region,” he said. “Israel will not allow steps against it without a response.”
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei has criticised the latest US sanctions against Iran- referred to as “Economic D-Day”.
“Those who prefer to appear ‘as obedient as shadows’ say: ‘This is fine.’ But hold on. It is absolutely not fine," he wrote in a post on X.
“When a bully declares that every bank, company, port, and government must choose between obeying Washington’s whims or facing American vengeance, this is no longer just about Iran.”
Syria's SDF dissolves as part of integration with Damascus
The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces has been dissolved, the armed militant group's leader said on Tuesday, a major step in the integration plan agreed on earlier this year with the Islamist-led government in Damascus.
"We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and announce with full responsibility its dissolution as an independent military force," SDF commander Mazloum Abdi said in a televised speech.
The government and the group, which helped defeat the Islamic State with U.S. backing and held parts of northern and eastern Syria, agreed in January to a phased integration of Kurdish fighters into the state, a plan Washington called a "historic milestone".
The deal came shortly after government forces under President Ahmed al-Sharaa launched a lightning offensive in January, taking swathes of the areas the SDF held.
Abdi said that the announcement followed an agreement with Sharaa after the integration of the group's forces into the army.
The Kurdish People's Protection Units, which formed the core of the SDF, had already been integrated within state forces with its commander, Sipan Hamo, appointed in March deputy defence minister for the country's eastern territories.
The SDF dissolution comes as the new leaders in Damascus seek to resolve internal strife and rebuild Syria, with support from Washington, after nearly 14 years of civil war and decades of isolation under former President Bashar al-Assad's rule.
US Secret Service aware of Iran threat against Barron Trump
The US Secret Service is aware of a video broadcast by Iranian state television discussing a potential plot to assassinate U.S. President Donald Trump's youngest son, a spokesperson said on Tuesday.
"The US Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees. Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence," Secret Service spokesperson Nate Herring said in an email.
A three-minute video broadcast by Iranian state TV discussed a potential plot to assassinate Barron Trump, 20, claiming that he was being monitored and alleging that a $10 million bounty had been offered for his killing.
The United States and Iran have kept up hostile rhetoric during a nearly six-month-old war started by the U.S. and Israel in February. Reuters reported earlier this month that the U.S. has received several warnings from Israel over the past year that Iran intended to assassinate  Trump, according to officials, including before a secret Air Force One ruse in Turkey.
Trump has described himself as "number one on the kill list for Iran."
Barron Trump and his mother First Lady Melania Trump [Getty]
Oman FM says to announce temporary Hormuz shipping corridor
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Tuesday that he hoped his country and Iran would soon announce the establishment of a temporary shipping corridor in the Strait of Hormuz after weeks of negotiations.
"I am hopeful that we will soon announce a temporary corridor for the Strait of Hormuz, as well as practical arrangements to restore safe navigation. Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course," Albusaidi said in a statement after meeting Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran.
UN chief 'greatly alarmed', Israeli forces enter UNRWA base
United Nations chief Antonio Guterres on Tuesday condemned an incursion by Israeli forces on a training center run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) in an east Jerusalem suburb.
"The Secretary-General is greatly alarmed at this development, as it will deprive young people of the vocational education they were receiving," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said.
He added that the training center "and other UNRWA premises are premises of the United Nations. They are inviolable and immune from any form of interference."
Oman's top diplomat held talks in Iran on Tuesday, Tehran said, as the two countries seek a way to regulate transit through the Strait of Hormuz, which has emerged as a flashpoint in the Middle East war.
"Oman's Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi met and talked with Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran," an Iranian foreign ministry statement said.
No further details of the meeting were immediately announced.
Katz vows to keep Israeli troops in Syria during visit
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz made a rare visit to troops in southern Syria on Tuesday, reiterating a pledge to keep forces in the area as long as there were "threats" to his country's security.
The visit comes a week after Israel bombed the disused Abu Duhur base in northwestern Syria, claiming it wanted to prevent Turkish troops deploying to the facility. Ankara has denied any visit to the site.
In southern Syria, Israeli forces have been stationed in a "security zone" since the fall of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
They occupy what was previously a buffer zone patrolled by the United Nations that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan since 1974.
"There is daily activity here to thwart threats, to eliminate remnants of the old regime, to prevent dangerous consolidation of the new regime," Katz said according to a video statement from his office.
"The message is clear to the president of Syria as well: when you wake up in the morning in your palace in Damascus, look up at Mount Hermon and see the [Israeli forces]-- you know we are here to protect our communities and our border," he added.
"As long as there are threats, the [Israeli forces] will remain here to guarantee our security -- this is what we have done and this is what we intend to continue doing in the future," Katz said.
Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria since the fall of Assad and made repeated incursions into Syrian territory.
Trump says executions of Iran protesters must stop
US President Donald Trump expressed outrage on Tuesday at the mounting number of executions in Iran of people allegedly involved in mass protests earlier this year before the Middle East war began.
"The failing Islamic Republic of Iran is not paying large segments of their military, while at the same time killing protesters, even when they are not protesting, at levels not seen before," he wrote on Truth Social.
"It is a humanitarian crisis of epic proportions, and must be stopped, NOW," he added.
It was not immediately clear what new information had spurred the early morning post, but there has been a steady increase in executions since the outbreak of the war on February 28.
The joint US-Israeli strikes which kicked off the war came weeks after the violent quelling of mass protests in Iran.
Rallies initially began in late December over outrage at the high cost of living, but rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, but attributed the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel.
Rights groups based abroad recorded a far higher toll and said the security forces had fired on demonstrators.
Airlines have largely resumed services through parts of the Gulf, but some destinations remain disrupted.
Dubai continues to be one of the most affected destinations, with several European and Asian carriers extending suspensions into October or later.
Multiple Lufthansa Group airlines maintain suspensions to destinations including Dubai and Beirut through late October.
British Airways, Air Canada, Singapore Airlines and Wizz Air have also extended suspensions on a range of Middle East routes. Air France is meanwhile moving towards resumption of its Middle East destinations.
Airlines moving toward resumption
Air France: Beirut flights are suspended until September 1, flights to Riyadh and Dubai suspended until August 25.
Oil down as traders weigh US sanctions threat against Iran
Oil prices slipped for a second day on Tuesday as traders judged the latest US warning of sanctions against Iran to have reduced the risk of renewed military strikes, after six months of war in the Gulf.
The measures appeared softer than analysts had expected, and were accompanied by news of further shuttle diplomacy as a key Pakistani mediator met with the Iranian president on Monday.
The news helped calm oil markets, with prices falling around three percent and the international benchmark Brent back below $90 a barrel.
The main US exchanges rose in early trading, matching earlier gains in Europe, though London slipped back into the red in the afternoon.
Talks to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have remained stalled for weeks, which had pushed oil prices up for most of August -- fuelling inflation fears and unnerving bond investors.
The US said expanded "secondary" sanctions would target Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors -- but gave no timeline and named no specific countries beyond Iran.
Long queues have formed at petrol stations across Tehran as motorists rush to refuel amid growing concerns over fuel supplies and the impact of Washington’s latest sanctions on Iran.
The developments come as the US intensifies economic pressure on Tehran, while Iranian officials insist the country is prepared to withstand the measures.
Follow our live coverage for the latest updates from Iran, the US and the wider region.

articles.title: U.S. senator visits Kyiv drone factory, praises innovation
articles.body:
- Sen. Richard Blumenthal visited Ukrainian drone manufacturer SkyFall in Kyiv, saying the company produces thousands of Vampire drones daily.
- SkyFall also builds Shrike FPV drones and P1-SUN Shahed interceptors used by Ukrainian forces.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal toured a Ukrainian drone production line in Kyiv and said the country is manufacturing “thousands” of attack drones every day, offering a rare on-the-record look from a sitting U.S. lawmaker at the scale of Ukraine’s wartime drone industry.
Blumenthal named the company as SkyFall, a Ukrainian defense technology firm, in a post on X that included video from inside the facility.
“SkyFall in Kyiv is doing cutting edge drone manufacturing & changing modern warfare. Its innovation & new technologies are powering Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s bloody slaughter,” Blumenthal wrote.
“Thousands of drones. These are Vampires produced every day here at SkyFall in Kyiv. It is just a miraculous way to defend the country. Innovative, ingenious, and this company is securing the future of Ukraine, but also changing modern warfare through its incredible work,” Blumenthal said in the video.
SkyFall builds several drone systems currently used by Ukrainian forces, including the Vampire heavy bomber drone, known on the front line as “Baba Yaga,” multiple configurations of the Shrike first-person-view drone, and the P1-SUN interceptor, designed to shoot down Shahed-type attack drones. The company also runs SkyFall Academy, a training center for drone pilots, technicians and instructors.
Blumenthal’s visit follows a similar trip by Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who toured a SkyFall production facility on July 11 and was shown the same three systems, along with unreleased technology the company plans to field on the battlefield. Graham said afterward that it would be a “huge mistake” for the United States not to work more closely with Ukraine on drone technology, and SkyFall said the two sides discussed potential areas of cooperation in defense innovation.
The back-to-back visits by two senior senators, one Democrat and one Republican, within weeks of each other signal a level of bipartisan congressional interest in Ukraine’s domestic drone industry that has been rare on other aid or policy questions tied to the war. Both lawmakers sit on committees with direct influence over U.S. defense spending and foreign assistance, and both used their visits to publicly argue for deeper U.S.-Ukrainian cooperation on unmanned systems technology rather than framing the trips around traditional military aid requests.
SkyFall has expanded its international profile over the past year, including a July agreement with U.S. defense company Auterion to supply 50,000 first-person-view drones equipped with autonomy software for the Ukrainian Armed Forces, and an earlier partnership with Airbus Defence and Space to jointly develop next-generation air defense technologies. The company also participated in the Ukrainian Pavilion at CES 2025 in Las Vegas.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Strikes on Wildberries and Refineries Could Push Moscow Toward Peace Talks, Stubb Says
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Strikes on Wildberries and Refineries Could Push Moscow Toward Peace Talks, Stubb Says
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Ukraine’s long-range strikes against Russian refineries and warehouses are increasing the economic cost of the war for Moscow and could help pressure Russia into peace negotiations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Stubb made the remarks at a press conference following the Coalition of the Willing summit in Kyiv, according to an RBC-Ukraine correspondent on August 24.
The Finnish president compared Ukraine’s current position with the situation a year earlier, arguing that Kyiv is now in stronger military, financial, and economic circumstances.
According to Stubb, maintaining that momentum requires continued military and financial assistance to Ukraine, including support for its ability to conduct long-range strikes inside Russia.
Stubb also pointed to what he described as changing attitudes toward the war among the Russian population. According to the Finnish president, 65% of Russians now say they want the war to end.
He specifically linked the shift in public sentiment to Ukrainian strikes on Wildberries warehouses in Russia, saying such attacks had contributed to a 10-percentage-point increase in the share of Russians favoring an end to the war.
Stubb argued that Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign is therefore not only militarily significant but could also increase domestic pressure on Moscow and ultimately influence the Kremlin’s willingness to negotiate.
The Finnish president’s remarks came as Ukraine has increasingly used domestically produced long-range drones and other weapons to target Russian oil refineries, logistics facilities, and other sites inside Russia, a campaign Ukrainian officials have described as “long-range sanctions.”
At the same time, Ukraine is working with its partners to further expand its long-range capabilities. The country is set to establish domestic production of Storm Shadow cruise missiles after the United Kingdom authorized the transfer of the necessary technology. British and French defense companies will also participate in developing the production capability.

articles.title: CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow. Here’s what we know.
articles.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow. Here’s what we know.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow. He flew in from Riga aboard a U.S. Air Force Boeing C-17 military transport plane that landed at Vnukovo Airport on the morning of Aug. 25. Around 7 p.m., it emerged that the American plane that had brought Ratcliffe had departed Moscow.
Ratcliffe is the first CIA director to visit Moscow since 2021. His predecessor, William Burns, traveled there that year amid a Russian military buildup near Ukraine’s borders. The trip is also the first visit to Russia by a U.S. administration official since January 2026.
The purpose of Ratcliffe’s visit remains unknown. The trip was never officially announced. The Kremlin claimed it had no knowledge of the American aircraft at Vnukovo and had no meetings scheduled with U.S. administration officials this week. Kremlin pool correspondent Alexander Yunashev said Vladimir Putin changed his work schedule amid Ratcliffe’s visit, canceling a large-scale event planned for Aug. 25. Axios reported that Ratcliffe came for talks, though it did not specify with whom or on what.
One theory holds that the visit may be connected to the release of Charles Zimmerman, an American convicted in Russia. Ksenia Sobchak reported this on her Telegram channel, Krovavaya Barynya (“Bloody Lady”), without citing a source. If true, Zimmerman would be the second American pardoned and sent home by Russian authorities within a month. The first was Robert Gilman, whose release without an exchange was seen as possible groundwork for a new round of peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv with U.S. participation.
Another theory holds that Ratcliffe discussed some sort of “important operation” in Moscow. The claim was posted by the Telegram channel Ukraine Context, which is close to Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency. The channel’s authors say preparations for the operation had been “conducted in secrecy for some time” and that its “results could significantly affect what happens next.”
A third theory is that Ratcliffe came to deliver a “warning” to Putin. The Wall Street Journal put it forward. According to the paper, the U.S. has gathered intelligence indicating that Russia has begun preparing for a mobilization to continue its war against Ukraine and may be planning to “test NATO’s resolve” by staging a provocation against alliance member states. The paper also suggested the visit could be tied to the war between the U.S. and Iran, a Russian ally. The day before, Washington announced a new campaign of economic pressure against Iran.
American journalist Michael Weiss also suggested Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow to warn against a possible Kremlin escalation against Europe and NATO. ”[It’s] linked to U.S. intelligence shared with Poles, Balts, and Scandinavians, and comes amid a noticeable uptick in suspected GRU [Russian military intelligence] sabotage operations and Russian drone activity,” Weiss said.
Amid the CIA director’s trip, the U.S. asked Ukraine not to strike Moscow. A source told Axios that ahead of Ratcliffe’s visit, Washington notified Kyiv that a high-level delegation would be arriving in the Russian capital and asked it to pause attacks. According to the Financial Times, the U.S. also asked Ukraine not to strike St. Petersburg and Russia’s northern regions through Aug. 26.
Ratcliffe’s visit sent the Moscow Exchange index swinging. News of his arrival pushed it up more than 3%, to 2,141.46 points. The index fell after reports that the plane had left Vnukovo.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: ‘Not an isolated incident’: Russian drones stalk Ukraine’s civilians in ‘human safaris’
articles.body:
‘Not an isolated incident’: Russian drones stalk Ukraine’s civilians in ‘human safaris’
The video of a Ukrainian cyclist being targeted and killed by a short-range drone posted – and later deleted – by the Russian military Friday left viewers outraged and shaken. But it’s not the first time that Russian drone operators have been accused of terrorising Ukrainian civilians by deliberately targeting them in “human safaris” denounced as a war crime by an independent UN commission.
First, he freezes, caught off guard. Then the young Ukrainian cyclist begins to backpedal awkwardly, his eyes never leaving the Russian drone that hovers ahead of him. It moves closer, and he swings his leg over the bike and tries to run. He doesn’t make it.
Even though the footage, posted Friday on the official Telegram account of the 3rd Army Corps of the Russian armed forces, cuts off before the moment of impact, the video’s description leaves no doubt of the outcome. The Russian soldiers congratulate themselves on having taken out an “enemy combatant” in the Ukrainian district of Kramatorsk, not far from the front line in the northern Donetsk region.
Two years of ‘human safaris’
But the cyclist was visibly unarmed, wearing civilian clothes and looked like any other young man riding his bike down a country road. Independent Russian media outlet Astra quickly accused the Russian military of trying to pass off an unarmed cyclist as a Ukrainian combatant.
The video spread swiftly across social media as influential accounts, including prominent Kremlin critic and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov, reposted the footage to denounce the Russian military’s apparent cruelty.
Less than 48 hours and hundreds of outraged comments later, the 3rd Army Corps took the video down.
It’s far from the first time that Russian drones laden with explosives and controlled from a distance have targeted civilians in Ukraine’s frontline regions. The Ukrainians have even found a term for these deadly drone hunts – “human safaris”.
“On the one hand, I'm very happy that there is more attention on this,” said Olga Tokariuk, a specialist in Ukraine at the British think-tank Chatham House. “On the other hand, this is not something new. This has been happening for two years. And the impunity that Russia faces for these attacks just means it can continue.”
Watch moreKherson under fire: The reality behind the Russian drone strikes
The “human safari” carried out by Russian drone operators seems to have begun in July 2024 in Kherson, a city on the banks of Dnipro River in the country’s south.
“Kherson in 2024 was the point at which isolated incidents developed into a sustained campaign,” said Will Kingston-Cox, a specialist in Russia and the Ukraine war at the International Team for the Study of Security in Verona. “Initially, small quadcopters followed individuals and vehicles and dropped explosives. Since then, we have seen FPV (first-person view) impact drones expanding the practice in scale, frequency and geography. Documented targets include pedestrians, cyclists, private cars, buses, ambulances and rescue workers.”
In Kherson, Russian forces installed on the opposite bank of the Dnipro can easily use short-range drones to target the population who had either remained in or returned to the city following its recapture by the Ukrainian army at the end of 2022.
‘Those seconds are so precious’
Numerous eye-witness accounts, including several reported by FRANCE 24’s Observers team, describe a climate of constant fear of being targeted and killed by a Russian drone.
Read moreHow Russian drones are terrorising civilians in Ukraine
Tokariuk, who wrote a report on the “human safaris” in 2025, said that people she’d interviewed in Kherson had spoken of being under a state of almost permanent tension.
“Something really striking that they told me was they would only go out there if the weather was bad – because drones cannot really operate in rain or snow or fog,” she said. “And they would also tell me they would drive really fast in their cars, because that maximises your chances of survival if you're hunted by a drone … People wouldn’t use their seatbelts when they're driving, because those seconds are so precious when they see a drone hovering above their car about to hit them, and they need to get out of the car really quickly.”
For its part, the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine condemned these “human safaris” as a war crime, for deliberately targeting a civilian population, and a potential crime against humanity, for its possible use as a tool to carry out forcible population transfers.
“They are targeting precisely not only civilians in their day-to-day life, but also hospitals and shops and very basic things that sustain day-to-day life for people,” said Ivan Klyszcz, a specialist in Russia at the Centre of Defence and Security in Tallinn, Estonia. “So there's definitely a pressure on the civilian population, and inevitably this leads to people to relocate. I cannot say that this is part of a larger plan for population transfer – but it is working out that way.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The UN commission reported that roughly 150 civilians had been killed and hundreds more wounded in Kherson region by short-range drones since the end of 2024.
Veronika Hinman, a specialist in the Ukraine war at the University of Portsmouth who has studied the use of drones in the conflict, said that while she wasn’t convinced the practice could be described as official army tactics, it certainly seemed tolerated by the military brass.
“I've been trying to think whether this could be just an isolated incident, whether we could consider these drone operators as 'bad apples' or rogue soldiers acting independently – or whether, if you look at the company itself that, they are remnants of an informal militia integrated into Russian forces later on,” she said. “But no, it doesn't seem anything like that. It's not an isolated incident.”
Cutting promos
Although Kherson remains ground zero for this grim practice, the fact that Friday’s cyclist was targeted by a drone in the distant Kramatorsk district shows that these “human safaris” have spread beyond the battered city.
Tokariuk said similar attacks had also been reported in Ukraine’s border region of Sumy, as well as in Kharkhiv, which sits across the border from Russia’s Belgorod region.
She maintained it was impossible that the drone operators didn’t know the people they were targeting were civilians.
“They know exactly what they’re doing,” she said. “The operators of these drones, they can see the real-time footage of who the drone is chasing.”
The practice is also likely a macabre way to train Russian troops to pilot the remote-controlled drones, Hinman said.
“Civilians are not protected. They are easy targets because of what they are wearing, as opposed to soldiers on the battlefield,” she said.
It may be that these “human safaris” can also allow Russian officers to made sure that the drone operators under their command won’t be overcome by remorse during combat operations. After all, soldiers who are apparently prepared to target old people leaving their homes and children playing in the street – cases documented by the UN commission – would likely be ready to carry out any other order.
Read moreZelensky calls on allies to cover €27 billion gap for Ukraine’s air defence needs
Hinman said that these videos also served encourage Russian viewers to donate money for the production and purchase of more drones to deploy at the front.
“One of the reasons why they post these on social media, why they make these social media posts, can be to show off what these drones are being used for to the people who fundraise for them,” she said.
By seemingly trying to pass off an unarmed civilian for a hardened Ukrainian soldier, Kingston-Cox said, Friday’s video appeared to have backfired – possibly, he said, explaining why it was later taken down.
“That discrepancy made the video both a propaganda liability and potentially important evidence,” he said. “Operational security concerns cannot be excluded, but reputational and legal containment appears more plausible – particularly because the footage appeared on a channel associated with the army rather than an anonymous pro-war 'miliblogger' (Russian military blogger) account.”
But Tokariuk said she didn’t think the controversy the video had caused would have any real impact on the Russian army’s use of these tactics.
“These drones are cheap to operate – they are flying the distances that they need to,” she said. “In those border regions they use drones because it works. It really keeps civilians in terror. It makes people flee.“
She said the seeming impunity that Russia had enjoyed for more than two years now over its “human safaris” made her worry that other states or actors could start to carry out their own version of the low-cost war crime.
“It is very easy to replicate elsewhere,” she said. “And civilians are completely defenceless against it.”
This article has been adapted from the original in French.

articles.title: Kremlin rejects idea of "buffer zone" in Donbas, saying region "belongs to Russia"
articles.body:
Kremlin rejects idea of "buffer zone" in Donbas, saying region "belongs to Russia"
Dmitry Peskov, press secretary for Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, has said the Kremlin rejects the proposal to create a "buffer zone" in Donbas as part of a joint Ukraine-US-EU plan, claiming that Ukrainian Donbas, which Russian forces are attempting to seize, "is a Russian region".
Source: Kremlin-aligned news agency Interfax
Quote from Peskov: "In this context, I would nevertheless say that Donbas is the territory of the Russian Federation, a constituent entity of the Russian Federation... And it is hardly possible for any third party to administer the regions of the Russian Federation."
Details: Meanwhile, the Kremlin spokesman claimed that Russia continues to wage the war because it sees no peaceful way to end it. "Russia remains open to peaceful solutions, but in the absence of such solutions, we continue the special military operation [the term Russians use for Russia's war against Ukraine – ed.]," he said.
Peskov once again made the unsubstantiated claim that the Kremlin "not only expects but is also convinced that victory will be achieved", although he added that "this will depend on the current situation".
Background:
- The Times reported that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had said Ukraine, together with the United States and Europe, had developed a number of proposals to end the war in Ukraine. The plan would include a ceasefire, the mutual withdrawal of Russian and Ukrainian troops from the front line and the creation of a buffer zone. "There are several more ideas from the American side, as far as we know. They want to find the right moment to share them. We are waiting for them," Zelenskyy said.
- On 22 August, Putin described Ukraine's proposals for a peaceful settlement as "exotic" and unacceptable to Russia.
- On 24 August, Zelenskyy said in an address to Ukrainians marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence that "the Russians must be brought to the negotiating table". "There finally must be sanctions that will make them howl. Ukraine must be given everything that will force them to end the war. And this is possible," the head of state said.
- Earlier, Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, said Putin does not want talks now and will be even less willing to negotiate once the cold weather arrives because he believes Ukrainians will not be able to survive the coming winter.
- On 14 August, Russia's Defence Ministry posted a photo of attack drones accompanied by a threat to "freeze" Ukraine this winter. The Strategic Communications Directorate of Ukraine's Armed Forces responded by promising to "keep warm by the fire of Russian oil refineries".

articles.title: How will Trump's economic 'D-Day' plan impact Iran's nuclear, ballistic missile threat? - analysis
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s threat of an “economic D-Day” against Iran sounded impressive but so far appears to have dropped to a bit of a whimper.
It is not clear that any strategic change took place vis-à-vis Iran on Monday, though if Washington decides to go head-to-head with Beijing over Iranian oil, and if China moves in America’s direction on the issue, those events could impact Tehran over time. But the keywords here are “economic,” “if,” and “over time.”
The real “D-Day” (June 6, 1944) was not an economic sanctions campaign; it was one of the largest military ground invasions of all time.
Trump’s unwillingness to use ground forces in Iran, even for targeted operations, such as securing the Strait of Hormuz or removing Iran’s 60% enriched uranium, cannot be covered up by using the catchphrase “D-Day” where it does not apply.
The United States may hope to coax Chinese President Xi Jinping into reducing the oil it gets from Iran, given that it purchases an estimated 90% of that oil, but Jinping has also said “No” plenty of times, and it is unclear what Trump can offer him to sell such an arrangement.
“If” China keeps buying Iranian oil, is the US really going to use force against Chinese ships to block them from moving through Hormuz?
As it is, there is evidence that China has figured out how to dodge America’s blockade in some cases with its shadow fleet maneuvering tactics.
No matter how well this goes, it is a strategy that will only work “over time” – it takes time and patience.
Can Trump own such a long-term campaign?
This will not wear down Iran in a few days or weeks, unless its leadership suddenly completely changes its colors.
Rather, this will only work if the United States and the West are ready to go all in on this strategy for months, if not longer.
Can Trump own such a long-term campaign, which so far is crippling him politically, along with the US economy?
The key question is not whether Iran is being increasingly hurt economically; certainly it is.
Nor is it whether Trump has managed for some weeks here and there to mitigate some of the gas price pains with some of his confounding public relations; sometimes he has.
But the basic economic picture in the US is dark, and if the Americans’ threshold for suffering is much lower than the Iranian regime’s threshold, which is likely the situation, Trump may ditch the strategy before it can work.
Prior to the war, US gas prices were as low as $2.80 a gallon.
They have reached as high as $4.50 since Iran began to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, dropped as low as $3.80 in July, and are now back up to $4.05.
Before the war, an estimated 100 or more ships sailed through Hormuz daily.
At a low point during the war, this dropped to an average of 20 ships exiting per day and 10 entering.
In July, the numbers temporarily jumped to an average of 50 exiting daily and 20 entering.
Now those numbers are back down to 20 exiting and 10 entering.
That is the broader picture, and oil shipping has been even worse, with estimates of average daily shipping down to around 10% of pre-war levels.
The official numbers do not tell the whole story. Both Iran and the US are running clandestine shipping operations, but if gas prices remain as high as they are, that is the bottom line, which could undermine the US’s staying power in this “economic suffering” contest.
Let’s say Israel benefits from the best-case scenario where Trump stays the course on an economic and maximum pressure campaign over the next several months or longer.
How would that make Israel safer from the nuclear and ballistic missile threats?
Such a campaign would reduce Iran’s support of terror proxies and prevent it from getting a strategic upper hand to blackmail the US and the West by using Hormuz as its new regular point to crunch everyone.
In a general sense, having less money could also make it harder to restore its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
But not really.
The debate around Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile program
Time and time again, Israel has seen that religious fanatics, from Iran to Hezbollah to Hamas, are ready to use any small amount of funds they receive to finance their most dangerous military options at the expense of helping their civilian populations.
Since the full-on part of the early 2026 war ended, Iran has been working at a furious speed to repair and rebuild aspects of its missile program and possibly aspects of its nuclear program.
And it has, at least in some months since the war ended, received billions of dollars from China and Russia – so there is money there.
The status of Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missiles program is hotly debated.
Israel certainly succeeded in setting Iran back on the nuclear issue in June 2025, given that 15 months have passed and the Islamic Republic is nowhere near developing a weapon in the near future.
It also set back Iran’s missile program, given that estimates were at one point that it had 2,500 to 3,000 missiles and the capacity to build 100 to 300 additional missiles per month, eventually reaching 5,000, 6,000, or even 8,000 missiles – and now it is down to under 1,000, possibly only several hundred.
Further, while how many new missiles it can produce now is debated, no one doubts that if enough time passes, and with help from China and Russia, the missiles could emerge once again as a separate existential threat from the nuclear program.
Trump’s minimum stated goal at the start of the war was to remove the Islamic Republic’s more than 400 kilograms of 60% enriched uranium.
That has not been accomplished.
How long do Israel, the US, and the West want to give the regime in Iran to figure out ways in which to charge forward on the nuclear or ballistic missile issues with whatever it has left?

articles.title: US asked Ukraine to refrain from striking Moscow during CIA chief's visit, source says
articles.body:
US asked Ukraine to refrain from striking Moscow during CIA chief's visit, source says
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
The U.S. asked Ukraine not to strike Moscow and St. Petersburg while CIA Director John Ratcliffe is visiting Russia, a person familiar with the situation told the Kyiv Independent on Aug. 25.
"They don't believe in the strength of (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's air defenses," they said, adding that Kyiv agreed to pause strikes against the cities between Aug. 24 and 26.
A U.S. official confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that Ratcliffe is scheduled to meet senior Russian officials, but it remains unclear what is on the agenda. The Kremlin has not officially commented on the visit.
This marks Ratcliffe's first known official trip to Russia. The CIA director has nevertheless maintained contact with his Russian counterpart, SVR chief Sergei Naryshkin, who has previously signaled readiness to meet the U.S. spy chief.
The Ukrainian side was told that a U.S. delegation would travel to Russia, but was not initially informed that Ratcliffe would be a part of it, a source told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian officials are expected to receive a debrief after the trip, though it is unclear whether the CIA director will travel to Kyiv in person, they said.
Earlier on Aug. 25, the Flightradar24 tracking service reported that a U.S. Air Force C-17 military transport plane departed Riga in the morning and landed at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport at around 10 a.m. local time.
The plane was previously stationed at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland — the base also used by Air Force One and other planes carrying top U.S. officials.
Shortly after the plane landed, Moscow media shared footage of a convoy of cars with U.S. diplomatic license plates driving through the city.
The U.S. and Russia have seen intensified bilateral contacts since U.S. President Donald Trump took office last January and pledged to negotiate a peace settlement in Ukraine.
Despite repeated visits by Trump's peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to Moscow, the negotiations have effectively stalled as both Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on territorial issues.
Both Witkoff and Kushner were expected to make their first visits to Ukraine this week, but the trip was postponed.
A source denied earlier reports that the envoys delayed the trip due to intensified Russian attacks, noting that Trump wanted to keep the diplomats close due to the unresolved standoff with Iran.
Ukraine's top negotiator, Rustem Umerov, spoke by phone with Witkoff on Aug. 23, and the latter promised to eventually travel to Ukraine, they added.
Despite the deadlock in peace talks, Washington and Moscow continue to keep their diplomatic channels open, which on Aug. 11 helped to broker the release of former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, who had been imprisoned in Russia for four years.
The CIA has previously played a role in prisoner exchanges between Russia and the U.S.

articles.title: CIA Director visits Russia for talks – media
articles.body:
Director John Ratcliffe of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has arrived in Russia for talks, CBS News reported Tuesday, citing sources.
"CIA Director John Ratcliffe is in Moscow, Russia, for meetings, sources familiar with the situation told CBS News on Tuesday," CBS News reporter Jennifer Jacobs said.
She did not provide any further details.
Commenting on Ratcliffe's visit to Russia, Viktoria Strakhova, an advisor to the President's Office, expressed the view that the trip could be related to a proposal regarding the so-called "buffer zone."
"As I understand it, Zelenskyy's plan is for Russia to put forward a proposal, while the U.S. explains the possible alternative consequences. I think, by the way, that Ratcliffe's visit is timed precisely for this purpose. The "pressure menu" includes sanctions and the late Lindsey Graham's bill. As for whether there are any issues regarding Starlink – I don't believe so," she said on Facebook.
She added that she does not expect the Russians to agree to the U.S. side's terms.
According to American journalist Michael Weiss, Ratcliffe is in Moscow to warn of an escalation in Russian actions against Europe and NATO. " Linked to U.S. intelligence shared with Poles, Balts and Scandinavians, and comes amid a noticeable uptick in suspected GRU sabotage operations and Russian drone activity," he said on X social media platform, adding that Ratcliffe is also the most pro-Ukrainian official in the administration responsible for assisting Kyiv in carrying out deep strikes.
The Wall Street Journal, in turn, suggests that Ratcliffe's visit is linked to reports of Russia's preparations for a mobilization this fall, and that his main task is to deliver a warning to Moscow.

articles.title: Ukraine slowly losing war without systemic changes and innovation – Fedorov
articles.body:
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov stated that the country is gradually losing the war against Russia and has only a few months to make decisions that could change the course of events. He made these remarks in comments to Reuters.
"I think that there's now a turning point which will determine our future trajectory, but it looks as though we're gradually, slowly losing," Fedorov said.
He added that Ukraine still has "every chance" to win, but it urgently needs a plan to end the war.
In his view, the main obstacles are the lack of a unified vision for victory, insufficient adoption of technology, as well as entrenched corruption and patronage networks.
Fedorov said the country has the potential to win thanks to the development of autonomous drones with artificial intelligence, low-cost interceptor missiles, and its own ballistic missile program; however, the state lacks a comprehensive strategy for their deployment. In his assessment, the effectiveness of state institutions is about five percent, which prevents the country from taking full advantage of available technological developments.
"Technologies exist already which could completely stop the Russians, but our absence of vision… means we do not apply them," he said.

articles.title: CIA chief in Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
articles.body:
CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
- Published
The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.
John Ratcliffe reportedly arrived in the Russian capital earlier on Tuesday. Neither Washington or Moscow have confirmed the nature of the visit or who he was due to meet.
In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.
Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday. It departed later on Tuesday.
BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment.
Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport.
It departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appeared to have landed in the Russian capital at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from FlightRadar24. It returned to Riga shortly before 17:00 GMT.
Footage on social media also purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow.
Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.
The trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, although he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow.
John Foreman, who served as a British military attaché to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme that the visit could be focused on "escalation management" given speculation recent drone activity in Germany could be linked to Russia.
He said: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."
Foreman said the trip could also concern the release of US detainees currently being held in Russia.
Ratcliffe played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine.
The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, as well as former US marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.
The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.
Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term.
Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.
Additional reporting by Washington correspondent Daniel Bush and BBC Verify

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with two missiles including ballistic one; 124 of 150 drones neutralized
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with two missiles including ballistic one; 124 of 150 drones neutralized
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched two missiles and 150 drones at Ukraine. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 124 unmanned aerial vehicles; hits were recorded at 17 locations.
Russia launched a ballistic missile, another missile and 150 drones at Ukraine overnight; 124 of them were shot down or suppressed, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Tuesday, according to UNN.
Details
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of August 25 (since 18:00 on August 24), the enemy attacked with an Iskander-M ballistic missile from Rostov Oblast, a Kh-31P guided aviation missile from Bryansk Oblast, as well as 150 Shahed-type attack UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera UAVs and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk – Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense shot down/suppressed 124 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera UAVs and drones of other types in the north, south and east of the country. Impacts by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 17 locations, as well as the falling of downed objects (debris) at 7 locations
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: South Korea pledges to help Trump revive talks with North Korea’s Kim
articles.body:
Advertisement
South Korea pledges to help Trump revive talks with North Korea’s Kim
Trump’s recent olive branch to Kim and criticism of Seoul have raised concerns of a strain on long-standing Asian alliances
2-MIN READ2-MIN

South Korea and the US agreed to maintain close coordination on efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea, days after Pyongyang rebuffed President Donald Trump’s overtures and launched a barrage of short-range ballistic missiles.
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a phone call late on Monday that Seoul would work to ensure that Trump’s recent messages lead to renewed US-North Korea discussions and peace on the Korean peninsula, Seoul’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Tuesday.
The US State Department issued only a brief statement on the phone call, which comes at a period of tension between the allies. Trump recently announced a scaling back of joint military exercises and praised nuclear-armed North Korea, while saying that Seoul had not helped his efforts to try to denuclearise Iran.
The State Department said Rubio and Cho discussed “a range of issues in the US-ROK Alliance”, referring to South Korea by the initials of its official name, the Republic of Korea.
“The secretary noted the need for the two countries to remain in close coordination on matters that are integral to the alliance,” it added.
In its statement, South Korea’s Foreign Ministry did not mention whether the diplomats reaffirmed their usual commitment to North Korea’s denuclearisation, despite their emphasis on the importance of cooperation on the North Korean nuclear issue.

articles.title: Kremlin denies planned talks with US envoys amid reports CIA head in Russia
articles.body:
Kremlin denies US talks amid reports CIA Director Ratcliffe in Russia
Washington reportedly alerted Ukraine to refrain from strikes until delegation leaves Moscow, US media reports.
The United States’ spy chief is reportedly visiting Moscow for meetings, according to US media outlets, even as the Kremlin says no talks with US envoys are planned this week.
CBS News, citing unnamed sources familiar with the situation, reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe was in the Russian capital on Tuesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items

- list 2 of 4Russian expert warns of impending social crisis as Ukraine death toll rises
- list 3 of 4Zelenskyy says wartime elections could ‘destroy’ Ukraine
- list 4 of 4UK to help Ukraine build Storm Shadow long-range missiles: Why it matters
Axios separately confirmed the highest-level visit by a Trump administration official to Russia since January, quoting a US official.
The outlets did not say whom he was meeting or what the talks are expected to cover. The CIA declined to comment, according to the Reuters news agency.
The news comes after a US military transport aircraft travelled from Riga to Moscow, according to flight-tracking websites.
Russia, meanwhile, said no talks between Moscow and US envoys are planned this week, as Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations remain stalled.
“No, there are no such plans,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a press briefing on Tuesday.
Asked about reports that a US military plane landed in Moscow on Tuesday morning, Peskov said he had “no such information”.
Earlier, data from Flightradar24 showed a US military C-17 travelling from the US to Latvia and then on to Moscow, having departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and landing at nearly 07:04 GMT.
Later, the plane believed to be carrying Ratcliffe departed Moscow, according to data on the flight-tracking website.
Ratcliffe’s reported visit comes as US-brokered talks aimed at ending Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have stalled. But Moscow earlier this month freed a former US Marine detained since 2022 amid concerns about his health.
Axios also reported that Washington informed Ukraine of a senior delegation traveling to Moscow in advance and asked it to suspend strikes until it leaves, quoting a source with knowledge of the matter.
The Iran war is also a live issue between Washington and Tehran’s ally, Moscow.
CIA Director Ratcliffe has been reportedly central to high-profile prisoner exchanges between the US and Russia since US President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, including the release of a US-Russian dual national, Ksenia Karelina.
If confirmed, the reports of his visit would mark the first such trip since then-CIA Director William Burns travelled to Moscow in 2021.

articles.title: The CIA director may have come to Moscow due to the threat of Russia escalating against NATO — journalist
articles.body:
The CIA director may have come to Moscow due to the threat of Russia escalating against NATO — journalist
Kyiv • UNN
Journalist Michael Weiss suggested that John Ratcliffe may have come to Moscow to warn Russia against escalating against Europe and NATO. He linked this to GRU and drone activity.
American journalist Michael Weiss suggested that CIA Director John Ratcliffe may have arrived in Moscow to warn the Russian leadership that further escalation against European countries and NATO is unacceptable. Weiss wrote this on the social media platform X, UNN reports.
According to Weiss, the possible visit by the CIA chief may be linked to U.S. intelligence information that Washington shared with Poland, the Baltic states, and Scandinavia.
"If I had to place a bet, I would say that Ratcliffe is in Moscow to warn about Russian escalation against Europe/NATO," Weiss wrote.
The journalist drew attention to a noticeable increase in the number of suspected sabotage operations linked to Russia's GRU, as well as activity by Russian drones in Europe. He mentioned Germany, Bulgaria, and Romania among the countries where similar incidents had been recorded.
In Weiss's view, the CIA director's possible trip is unlikely to be related exclusively to potential prisoner exchanges.
"You don't need the CIA director for prisoner exchanges," he noted.
Weiss also described Ratcliffe as one of the most pro-Ukrainian members of the U.S. administration and said that he had played a role in assisting Kyiv with carrying out long-range strikes. The journalist drew a parallel with the events of 2021, when then-CIA Director William Burns traveled to Moscow on the eve of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"The context here is important: Bill Burns traveled to Moscow in 2021 to warn Putin against... invading Ukraine," Weiss wrote.
We remind you
The American Boeing C-17 that transported John Ratcliffe to Moscow departed from Vnukovo for Riga. Before the visit, the United States asked Ukraine to suspend strikes.

articles.title: “A Few Arrived. But We Need More”: Zelenskyy Confirms Ukraine Received Patriot Missiles
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
“A Few Arrived. But We Need More”: Zelenskyy Confirms Ukraine Received Patriot Missiles
Ukraine has received additional missiles for Patriot air defense systems, several Crotale systems with accompanying missiles, and AIM missiles as part of new agreements with international partners, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during a meeting with Estonian President Alar Karis in Kyiv.
The agreements were reached during the Coalition of the Willing summit in Kyiv and are aimed at strengthening Ukraine’s ability to defend its airspace against Russian attacks, as reported by RBC-Ukraine correspondent on August 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We received—I won’t say from which country—confirmation of the transfer of several Crotale air defense systems and missiles for them. And we also received AIM missiles. These are very important missiles for us; we use them to shoot down enemy missiles,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president also confirmed that the country had received an additional batch of missiles for US-made Patriot air defense systems, although he did not disclose either the supplier or the number delivered.
“And, to be honest, I also won’t say from which country, but a few more missiles for Patriot have arrived. I can’t say how many, but a few. We need more,” Zelenskyy said.
The additional air defense supplies come as Ukraine continues to seek more interceptors and systems from its partners to protect cities and critical infrastructure from Russian missile and drone attacks.
Beyond strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, the Coalition of the Willing summit also resulted in new targeted assistance packages for individual Ukrainian regions and key sectors of the economy.
“We received [support] from Belgium, from Denmark—they are focused on the Mykolaiv direction. Estonia supports Zhytomyr,” Zelenskyy said.
According to the president, coalition members also agreed to support several projects for Ukrainian veterans. Belgium and Germany separately announced energy assistance packages intended to strengthen Ukraine’s energy sector.
Sweden, meanwhile, will provide a significant financial package to support the production of Ukrainian drones, Zelenskyy said.
The new Patriot deliveries come amid broader concerns over the availability of interceptors among Ukraine’s European partners. European countries have struggled to identify sufficient stocks as Kyiv prepares for the possibility of intensified Russian strikes during the winter.
Ukraine is seeking hundreds of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors, but limited inventories among its partners have complicated efforts to secure the quantities required.

articles.title: Poland Signs Largest-Ever Piorun MANPADS Contract with Four European Armies
articles.body:
Poland has signed the largest-ever contract to supply Piorun MANPADS to Lithuania, Latvia, Norway, and the Polish Armed Forces.
According to Poland’s Ministry of Defense, the €1.86 billion framework agreement was signed at the MESKO plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna, south-central Poland.
The deal covers the delivery of several thousand Piorun man-portable air-defense systems.
More than 80% of the order will be delivered to the Polish Armed Forces, while the remainder will go to Lithuania, Latvia, and Norway under the EU’s SAFE program, a financing mechanism for joint defense procurement.
Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said this is the first agreement of its kind in which the consortium consists of allied governments rather than companies.
The agreement, signed between Poland’s State Agency for Armaments and MESKO S.A., also includes personnel training and logistics support packages.
The Piorun man-portable air-defense system (MANPADS) is a very short-range air-defense system designed to counter low-flying threats, including aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
The missile system is a major modernization of its predecessor, the Grom, which was introduced into the Polish Armed Forces in 1995. The Grom itself was developed on the basis of the Soviet Igla-1 and Igla man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS).
Development of the Piorun took place from 2010 to 2015. As part of the modernization, the cooled, stabilized infrared homing seeker was significantly improved using modern electronic components. The seeker was given higher resolution and became four times more sensitive. The seeker uses argon as a coolant.
The Piorun system weighs 16.5 kg, of which 10.5 kg is the missile. The missile is 1.596 m long and carries an enhanced 1.82 kg warhead. It can engage aerial targets at altitudes of 10 to 4,000 m and at ranges of 500 to 6,500 m from the operator.
In addition to the countries covered by the framework agreement, Estonia, Belgium, Moldova, Georgia, and Sweden also operate the system.
Ukraine has successfully used the Polish MANPADS in combat since 2022, using them to shoot down several Russian helicopters, aircraft, cruise missiles, and drones.

articles.title: Putin adviser claims Ukraine planned to invade Russia on 8 March 2022, so Russia attacked first
articles.body:
Putin adviser claims Ukraine planned to invade Russia on 8 March 2022, so Russia attacked first
An adviser to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin has come up with yet another justification for Russia's war, claiming that Ukraine had planned to invade Russia on 8 March 2022, prompting Moscow to pre-empt it by attacking first.
Source: The Moscow Times, citing an interview with Anton Kobyakov, Putin's adviser and executive secretary of the Eastern Economic Forum organising committee, given to TASS, a Kremlin-aligned Russian news outlet
Details: The Russian official claimed that at the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian troops discovered documents at an abandoned headquarters of one of the Ukrainian Armed Forces' Territorial Defence brigades indicating that Kyiv was preparing to attack Russia on 8 March 2022.
"We beat them to it by two weeks," Kobyakov said, referring to Russia's invasion of peaceful Ukraine on 24 February 2022.
Putin's adviser claimed that Kyiv had wanted to "present the war as a gift" for International Women's Day and that Russia had attacked first "thanks to the foresight of the Russian leadership".
As usual, the Russian official also mentioned World War II while making these bizarre claims.
"As the president [Russian ruler Putin – ed.] said earlier, there will never again be a 22 June in our history [22 June 1941 was the day Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union – ed.]," Kobyakov added.
He also reiterated previous accusations that the West had "disguised itself as a supporter of the Minsk agreements" while actually "preparing Ukraine for war".
According to Kobyakov's version of events, the West supposedly intended to arm Kyiv and push it towards a military solution to the "conflict in Donbas" [as Russia describes its occupation of Ukrainian territories – ed.].
Why this matters: Russia invaded Ukraine and occupied the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and parts of Donbas as early as 2014.
In 2022, Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, attacking peaceful cities and towns across the country with missiles and bombs during the night.
Notably, in the early days of the full-scale invasion, Russian propagandists actively circulated claims that "Russia would take Kyiv in three days", while Russian soldiers advancing on the capital carried parade uniforms with them, intending to march down Khreshchatyk, the main street of Kyiv, after those supposed "three days".
However, as of late summer 2026, Russian forces have still failed even to reach the administrative borders of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts.
Throughout this period, the Russian authorities have invented various justifications for starting the war, claiming, among other things, that NATO intended to attack Russia and alleging the existence of "biolaboratories" in Ukraine. Their claims have even extended to absurd stories about "combat mosquitoes" and a "dirty bomb".
In 2023, Russia unveiled a rewritten history textbook containing false claims about the war in Ukraine.
