articles.title: Putin signed three secret decrees on the day of the CIA director’s visit to Moscow, Russian media report
articles.body:
Putin signed three secret decrees on the day of the CIA director’s visit to Moscow, Russian media report
Kyiv • UNN
Putin signed decrees No. 605–607, which were not published. Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow may have concerned mobilization, a provocation against NATO or an exchange.
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin signed three secret decrees amid the unexpected and unannounced visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe. The Moscow Times reports this, citing the Russian legal information portal, according to UNN.
Details
According to the portal, on August 25, Putin signed three open and published decrees — numbers 608, 609, and 610. Two of them concern a change of Russia’s ambassador to Iraq, while another changes the composition of commissions dealing with people with disabilities and veterans.
At the same time, Putin’s latest decree, signed the day before, on August 24, is numbered 604. It allows the state to take virtually any facilities and enterprises under “temporary administration” if their owners have not provided adequate protection against UAV strikes.
Thus, three more of Putin’s decrees were signed but were not published on the portal and are classified: numbers 605, 606, and 607.
During his visit to Moscow, the first since the start of the invasion of Ukraine, the CIA chief met with Putin — for this purpose, the president canceled one of the events for which “hundreds of people” had been preparing, Kremlin pool correspondent Alexander Yunashev reported.
It remains unclear what exactly was discussed in the talks. The Wall Street Journal writes that Ratcliffe may have delivered a warning to Putin in connection with U.S. intelligence showing that the Kremlin is preparing a new round of mobilization and a possible provocation against NATO. The iPaper links Ratcliffe’s visit to a possible prisoner exchange.

articles.title: Putin authorizes the seizure of  corporate assets that the government deems to be “insufficiently protected against drones”
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin has authorized the imposition of temporary state control over the property of companies in cases where state authorities determine that firms are not adequately protecting important facilities, including against drone attacks. Putin signed Decree No. 604, “On Measures to Ensure the Security of Critical Infrastructure Facilities of the Russian Federation,” on Aug. 24. The document was published on the country’s official legal information portal and has entered into force.
Grounds for imposing temporary control may include failure to take security measures or a delay in taking them, the violation of established requirements, creating a threat to the facility’s normal operation, or even a delay in restoring it after damage was incurred. The decree separately mentions “ineffective implementation of measures” aimed at preventing drone attacks.
Russian authorities will be able to place all or part of a company’s movable and immovable property, its securities and stakes in Russian legal entities, and its property rights under temporary control. The decision will be made by the government on Putin’s instructions. The Federal Agency for State Property Management (Rosimushchestvo) will step in as the temporary manager by default, unless replaced by a different organization. The manager will receive all relevant ownership powers other than the right to dispose of the transferred property. The decree does not limit the duration of temporary control, which can likewise be terminated by the government on the president’s instructions.
The decree defines “critical infrastructure facilities” as enterprises in the fuel and energy sector (including nuclear facilities), communications facilities, as well as utility, transport, and logistics infrastructure. The list remains open-ended, however, and the mechanism can also be applied to other facilities that authorities deem to be of “particular importance” for Russia’s security, economic stability, or the population’s livelihood.
The decree comes amid a sharp increase in Ukrainian attacks on Russian industrial and logistics infrastructure. Oil refineries have been a constant target of Ukrainian drones since early 2024, with the intensity of the strikes increasing in 2025. In 2026, Ukraine further scaled up the campaign. As the Financial Times reported, in the first half of the year alone, Ukrainian drones successfully struck Russian refineries at least 194 times — at 11 times the rate in the same period of 2025. By April, the monthly average of successful strikes on refinery production facilities and tank farms exceeded ten and subsequently held at roughly that level. Following the attacks, some refineries scaled back or completely halted oil processing for extensive periods, sometimes taking weeks to return to normal operation. Notably, some facilities have been hit multiple times.
Three days before the decree was signed, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak instructed oil companies to revise refinery maintenance schedules in order to avoid exacerbating the fuel shortage. Now, a delay in restoring facilities could have direct consequences for owners, as Putin’s decree explicitly names the untimely restoration of critical infrastructure after damage as grounds for imposing temporary control over a company’s property.
Since July 18, the warehouse infrastructure of the major online retailer Wildberries has also come under systematic attack. By Aug. 19, The Insider had counted 21 attacked marketplace facilities across 16 Russian regions and annexed Simferopol, affecting a combined storage area of about 2.3 million square meters. Fourteen facilities covering about 1.77 million square meters sustained significant damage, forcing the company to relocate some of its operations to other sites. Warehouse employees were killed and injured in several attacks. Volodymyr Zelensky has stated that the targeted logistics centers were used to supply the Russian army with drone production components, navigation equipment, and gear.
On Aug. 22, Ukrainian drones hit a logistics facility of another online retailer, Ozon, for the first time. The target of that strike was a warehouse in Chapayevsk, Samara Region. Then, on Aug. 23, a strike hit a facility in Orenburg, and overnight into Aug. 24, drones struck Ozon warehouses in Dagestan, Adygea, Krasnodar Krai, and Stavropol Krai. Fires broke out at the facilities near Krasnodar and Makhachkala, forcing them to halt operations.

articles.title: Russia hits Ukrainian cruise missile launch site – MOD (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russia hits Ukrainian cruise missile launch site – MOD (VIDEO)
The Russian military has struck a launch site for Ukraine’s long-range FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, the Defense Ministry said on Tuesday. Kiev has used Flamingos in attacks deep inside Russia.
The site was targeted with two Iskander cruise missiles and seven Geran-4 Seeker attack drones, according to the ministry.
“The target has been hit,” it said, adding that the strike triggered a major fire and “a massive fuel spill… burning over an area of approximately 40,000 square meters.”
The MOD also released drone footage purporting to show a massive fire engulfing the launch site after the attack.
In separate strikes, Russian forces also hit Ukrainian drone assembly and storage facilities, according to the ministry.
The Russian military has intensified long-range strikes on targets in Ukraine in response to repeated Ukrainian attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure inside Russia. Moscow has condemned Kiev’s drone and missile strikes, including attacks deep inside Russian territory, as acts of terrorism intended to compensate for Ukrainian setbacks on the battlefield.
Russia maintains that it does not deliberately target civilians and that its strikes are directed at military facilities and infrastructure supporting Ukrainian forces.
Last week, the Russian military struck an industrial facility belonging to Ukrainian weapons manufacturer Fire Point, which produces Flamingo missiles and other weapons. The plant manufactured components for long- and medium-range drones and was also used to assemble and store boosters for the cruise missiles, according to the MOD.
Fire Point has been promoted by Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky during trips to Western countries as the manufacturer of some of the nation’s “most successful” weapons. Over the weekend, a Russian volunteer air-defense unit shot down one of the supposedly state-of-the-art Flamingo missiles with machine-gun fire, according to Kursk Region Governor Aleksandr Khinshtein.
Fire Point has been linked to Zelensky’s former business partner, Timur Mindich, who has been dubbed ‘Zelensky’s wallet’ in Ukraine. Mindich fled the country last year after being named as a key suspect in a major corruption scandal.

articles.title: Russian military confirms classified satellite launch from Plesetsk
articles.body:
- Russia launched a classified military satellite from Plesetsk on August 24, a day after Ukrainian drones reached the surrounding region.
- Russian officials confirmed the satellite reached orbit but did not disclose its identity or mission.
Russia launched a classified military satellite from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on August 24, the country’s Ministry of Defense said, a day after Ukrainian drones reached the surrounding Arkhangelsk region in an apparent attempt to disrupt the launch. A Soyuz-2-1b rocket lifted off from Site 43, Pad 3, at 05:40 Moscow time.
Russian officials said the payload, listed only under the generic designation “Kosmos,” reached orbit as planned and that ground stations established telemetry contact with the satellite. The Ministry of Defense did not identify the spacecraft’s mission or specifications.
Ukrainian and Russian monitoring channels reported drones over Arkhangelsk region on August 23, with local officials describing the targets as “strategic facilities.” The Russian monitoring channel Locator Russia said at least two drones reached the vicinity of Plesetsk, and residents in the area filmed footage of drones overhead, according to the Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi. Governor Alexander Tsybulsky of Arkhangelsk region ordered residents to take shelter and said mobile internet service would be suspended, without disclosing the outcome of the attack. Russian authorities said 40 drones were shot down over the region in total.
It was the first reported case of Ukrainian drones reaching Arkhangelsk region, according to Militarnyi. Roscosmos director general Dmitry Bakanov said in April that Ukrainian forces had previously attempted a drone attack on Plesetsk during preparations for a March 25 satellite launch, an attack he said Russian space and air defense units repelled.
Plesetsk is Russia’s primary launch site for military satellites and has also been used to test the Sarmat intercontinental ballistic missile, according to Militarnyi. The site has hosted multiple Soyuz-2 and Angara rocket launches in 2026 carrying military satellites and batches of Rassvet-series communications satellites, built by the Russian company Bureau 1440.
Similar warnings reappeared in mid-August for a period between August 19 and August 30, overlapping with separate restriction notices tied to a presumed Angara-1.2 launch. On August 15, authorities in the Komi Republic announced closures of the Vashka and Zheleznodorozhny rocket-debris impact zones, sites previously used for GLONASS satellite launches on Soyuz rockets, without specifying an exact launch window beyond “the second half of August.” A similar warning followed on August 21 from officials in the Tyumen region regarding a debris impact zone in the Uvatsky district.

articles.title: Ukraine has received missiles for Patriot systems but needs more, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Ukraine has received missiles for Patriot systems but needs more, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine has received missiles for Patriot air defence systems and AIM missiles following recent meetings in the NB8 and Coalition of the Willing formats.
Source: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine
Details: "To be honest, some Patriot missiles have also arrived. I cannot say how many, but some. We need more," Zelenskyy said during a press conference with Estonian President Alar Karis in Kyiv on 25 August. He did not specify which type of missiles Ukraine received.
According to the Ukrainian Defence Ministry, Patriot systems can use three types of missiles: PAC-2, PAC-3 CRI and PAC-3 MSE. PAC-2 missiles are primarily designed to engage aircraft and cruise missiles, while PAC-3 CRI and PAC-3 MSE can intercept ballistic assets.
As the Defence Ministry noted, AIM missiles have been in service with the Ukrainian Armed Forces for several years and are launched both from F-16 fighter jets and from ground-based NASAMS air defence systems. Ukraine uses AIM-9 Sidewinder, AIM-120 AMRAAM and AIM-7 Sparrow missiles to engage aerial assets.
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine had received confirmation that several Crotale air defence systems and missiles for them will be delivered.
Crotale NG is a French short-range surface-to-air missile system designed to engage aerial assets at low and very low altitudes. France has previously supplied Ukraine with two such systems.
Background: Earlier, Zelenskyy said that the United States will supply Ukraine with missiles for Patriot air defence systems every month.

articles.title: Chernihiv Oblast hit by 45 Russian attacks as 5 killed, dozens injured across Ukraine in past day
articles.body:
Chernihiv Oblast hit by 45 Russian attacks as 5 killed, dozens injured across Ukraine in past day
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least five people and injured 99 others over the past day, local authorities said, with Chernihiv Oblast among the hardest hit after Russia launched a wave of strikes following Ukraine’s Independence Day.
Russia launched an Iskander-M ballistic missile, a Kh-31P guided missile, and 150 drones at Ukraine, the Air Force said. As of 9 a.m., air defenses had downed or suppressed 124 drones, while strikes were recorded at 17 locations. The attack was still ongoing at the time of the report.
In Chernihiv Oblast, 38 people were injured as Russian forces carried out 45 attacks across the region, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
In the city of Chernihiv, 25 people were injured in a strike on a high-rise residential building. The blast also shattered windows in nearby residential and administrative buildings and damaged more than 20 cars.
Later in the evening, a Russian attack drone struck a building in the center of the city of Mena that houses telecommunications operators, injuring 12 people, including four teenagers. Three people were hospitalized in moderate condition.
"Another absolutely cynical Russian strike — the city center, many people, purely civilian objects all around," Chaus said.
Russian forces also launched waves of Gerbera and Geran-type drones at Koriukivka overnight, striking several local businesses and damaging warehouses, outbuildings, and trucks. A 15-year-old girl was injured.
Russian drones also struck a woodworking enterprise, the Yalivshchyna regional landscape park, and open areas in Chernihiv, while critical infrastructure across the region was also hit, Chaus said.
Elsewhere across Ukraine, Russian attacks continued to cause civilian casualties.
In Kherson Oblast, two people were killed and 23 others, including one child, were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were killed, while one woman was injured in attacks on Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding district, Governor Ivan Fedorov said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, one person was killed and 13 others, including a 13-year-old girl, were injured in Russian attacks, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks injured 15 people, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
Three people were injured in Russian attacks across Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, local authorities said.
In Sumy Oblast, five civilians, including a 14-year-old girl, were injured in Russian attacks, local authorities said.
In Kyiv, one woman was injured after debris from a Russian drone hit a 16-story residential building in the Holosiivskyi district, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The strike damaged walls and shattered windows on the 14th floor.

articles.title: SOUTHCOM Conducts First Drug Boat Strike Under New Counter-Cartel Task Force
articles.body:
U.S. Southern Command recently announced its first lethal strike on a suspected narco-trafficking vessel in two months, and the first under a newly formed permanent counter-cartel task force. The U.S. is also reportedly planning to transfer MQ-9 drones to Colombia to bolster its counter-cartel efforts.
On Aug. 23, Joint Task Force-Western Hemisphere “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific,” according to a SOUTHCOM social media post. The strike happened in the Eastern Pacific and killed two alleged narco-terrorists.
“When I ordered the establishment of Joint Task Force-Western Hemisphere, it was precisely for this purpose: to accelerate, synchronize, and execute lethal actions against these destabilizing narco-terrorist networks,” Marine Corps Gen. Francis L. Donovan, SOUTHCOM commander, said in a statement. “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists—disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership, and eliminating cartel terror across the region.”
A SOUTHCOM spokesperson declined to comment on the strike, citing operational security reasons. An Air Forces Southern spokesperson did not immediately respond to a query.
As of this most recent attack, there have been 67 strikes since Sept. 2, 2025, killing 223 people. Many of the videos released by SOUTHCOM appear to be from drones, and MQ-9s are known to be stationed in the region. SOUTHCOM has declined to say what assets it has used in the strikes.
This first strike under the new task force comes just a few days after the Colombian newspaper El Colombiano reported Aug. 18 that the U.S. will transfer three MQ-9 Reaper drones to Colombia for use in its escalating war on cartels in the country.
“This transfer will also most likely require significant U.S. assistance on the training and doctrine side to allow Colombia to effectively integrate these platforms into their joint operations,” Henry Ziemer, a fellow with the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine
The benefit of Colombia operating its own MQ-9s would be freeing up more assets for SOUTHCOM, Special Operations Command-South, and the 12th Air Force to conduct the backbone of the combatant command’s work in the region—intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Norm Seip, former Air Forces Southern commander, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Having the drones under Colombian control also widens the U.S. intelligence network in the region, as they’ll likely be coordinating their flights with AFSOUTH’s 612th Air Operations Center, which recently hosted Ecuadorian Air Force intelligence officers for the first time during the region’s largest military exercise, PANAMAX, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.
SOUTHCOM still has other strike assets for the region, such as the AC-130J gunships located at Comapala, El Salvador, which has been reported as a hub for the Eastern Pacific air campaign against cartels, Ziemer said.
Larger Moves
The drone transfer news came shortly after Colombia, a previous holdout, agreed to join the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition—a 19-member group aligned with U.S. objectives in the region to combat cartels.
This marks the first known time that a Latin American nation has been armed with the MQ-9. Colombia did begin arming its military’s smaller, tactical drones in response to criminal gangs conducting more than 200 drone attacks on military personnel since 2024.
The move to put SOUTHCOM on a more aggressive footing under JTF-WH follows President Donald Trump’s shifting of the National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy last year to prioritize Western Hemisphere operations.
On Aug. 12, during PANAMAX in Panama, students from the U.S. Naval War College’s Maritime Advanced Warfighting School presented an update to a report requested by Donovan to the commander and Panamanian Minister of Public Security Frank Alexis Ábrego on developing “a joint, combined and interagency defense of identified strategic terrain in the region,” according to a NWC release.
Siep said the report itself wasn’t unusual and likely also stood as another “optic” for the region.
“It sends a couple of messages,” Seip said. “One, to those that are thinking that it’s business as usual with regard to what they may be doing, that is not in line with how SOUTHCOM wants to do business. We’re out there looking at the strategic level of various things that are of our interest to the command there, as well as certainly advertises to the United States taxpayers that, ‘hey SOUTHCOM is growing their game with capability, and here’s one way that we’re doing that’ from a standpoint of intellectual capital that’s being expended for this particular project.”
Though the “strategic terrain” was not identified in the release, Ziemer believes that since it was presented in Panama during the major exercise, it likely relates to the Panama Canal and other critical infrastructure.
“It does reflect a growing interest in SOUTHCOM’s area of responsibility from a U.S. defense planning perspective,” Ziemer said.
Effective Strikes
Donovan testified to Congress in March that while the drug boat strikes will be a part of the overall strategy to counter cartels, they might not be the most effective.
“Putting total systemic friction from point of production to point of delivery … I believe that actually kinetic strikes will be one of the many tools, and probably not the most effective tool, when we actually look at it as more of a campaign approach,” Donovan said at the time.
Seip said he agreed strikes are not the most effective tool, but they have a place in the overall mission to create the systemic friction that Donovan is seeking.
“It may be that these types of strikes, whether you have a positive or negative opinion of them, but these types of strikes may fit into what he’s trying to accomplish,” Seip said.
Part of that is not only hitting those specific boats but also sending a message: “You will not be allowed to operate and roam freely in the waters of South and Central America without consequences,” said Seip, president of the D.C. think tank American Security Project.
While experts say the strikes have not made a large impact on drugs flowing to the United States, the strikes are likely to continue.
“Neither the White House nor SOUTHCOM wants to foreclose the option to carry out future strikes against trafficking targets at sea, even as they recognize this strategy has not had the desired effect on drug trafficking flows,” Ziemer said. “Going forward, I would expect to see these kinds of strikes continue, albeit more sporadically.”

articles.title: Ex-Pussy Riot activist Rita Flores says Russia’s FSB forced her to inform on performance artist Pavel Krisevich. He found out from her interview and wrote to tell her she’s forgiven.
articles.body:
Ex-Pussy Riot activist Rita Flores says Russia’s FSB forced her to inform on performance artist Pavel Krisevich. He found out from her interview and wrote to tell her she’s forgiven.
Former Pussy Riot member and activist Rita Flores (real name Margarita Konovalova) said on August 24 that FSB officers recruited her in early 2023. According to Flores, security officials threatened to kill her family, and under that pressure she agreed to cooperate and gather information on contemporary artists and political activists, including Pussy Riot members. Among other things, Flores was ordered to draw information out of street artist Philippenzo (Filipp Kozlov) and performance artist Pavel Krisevich and to inform on them. Flores claimed she tried to hint to Krisevich and his wife, Elena, that a new criminal case was being prepared against him, and that she played an indirect part in his departure from Russia in late 2025. She was not able to leave the country herself until mid-August 2026. Meduza asked Krisevich about his friendship with Flores and what changed when he learned of her ties to the FSB.
Warning: This text contains profanity.
— Did you know Rita was planning to give an interview about her recruitment?
— That was news to me. Even after I left, Rita and I kept messaging each other as if nothing had happened. I didn’t know anything.
It was only lately that she dropped out of sight for a long stretch and stopped answering messages. It seemed like either something had happened or she was just offline for a while — which she’s been doing sometimes lately.
It hit me pretty hard — that this is how things really are.
— Before the interview came out, did she consult you at all, ask your advice, or say she was planning to reveal something like this?
— No.
— Did you have any suspicions that something was wrong? Were there rumors?
— Not until the very end. I could understand Rita’s position — that she stayed in Russia even in 2025. Well, not everyone wants to emigrate. We talked, we met up in person. Rita said she didn’t want to leave at all, despite the pressure. She’d given up activism, she said, and wanted a quiet family life, a child, that sort of thing.
I stayed in Russia until 2025 myself. There was an understanding: if you keep a relatively low profile and don’t stick your neck out, you still have some room to live your life. So I didn’t see anything suspicious.
Though people did say, “Look, Rita’s been in Russia this whole time, it’s all very strange.” It didn’t seem strange to me — I was in exactly the same position [there] before I left, even with the constant arrests. But I never suspected Rita.
— Flores says in the interview that she tried to pick a fight with you, and when that didn’t work, she used your wife, Elena, to do it. According to Rita, this was her way of trying to persuade you to leave together. How did it look from your side?
— I don’t remember Rita picking a fight with me at all. And my wife never told me Rita had written her anything like that either. That part of the interview sounds a bit strange to me. Maybe there were hints that I should leave, and I just didn’t pick up on what Rita considers a fight.
There was never any serious information in our messages, not even details about the performance at the missile [monument]. I told Rita about that in person, and it all lines up [with her account in the interview].
You can imagine what Rita’s role was. She told her handlers that something was being planned, though it wasn’t clear where. And then her handlers filled in the rest with some kind of FSB surveillance once I actually went to the site.
— So you don’t recall Rita Flores communicating with you in any unusual way after your release in 2025?
— The only thing that seemed suspicious to me after Rita’s interview came out was that she kept telling me I should get in touch with [Marat] Gelman and sell paintings through him, that kind of thing. I told her that contacting Gelman while I was still in Russia was dangerous and would end badly. But Rita kept coming back to it.
Given the context of the search in the Marat Gelman case in April 2025, it all came together for me. FSB officers didn’t find anything that time and left me alone. I wrote to Rita just now and asked her — was she trying to push this somehow? I suspected she might have been doing it deliberately, on her handlers’ orders, to get me connected to Gelman. But now that she’s free, she denies doing anything of the kind. I’ll trust that, since I have no other information right now.
Other than that, it was typical conversation among anti-war Russians. These days, everyone in Russia is careful not to reveal much. Mostly we talked about fairly trivial things: how people were doing, how they were coping, what their plans were.
— What were relations like within the art scene in Russia before you left? How strong was the mutual suspicion, the fear that someone might inform on someone else?
— I think it’s the same as with everyone. People don’t tend to suspect acquaintances and friends they’ve known a long time.
I don’t interact much with the art crowd, because their main problem isn’t suspicion of each other over cooperating with the cops — it’s mutual envy and hatred.
So I mostly crossed paths with old acquaintances and friends. I talked more with activists. Activists have their own precautions — they work in human rights, and that requires care.
In my own work, in my performances, I always had to tell someone close to me or an acquaintance what I was planning — to see their reaction. Or to make myself feel that if I didn’t go through with what I planned, I’d be ashamed — since I’d told people about it and then failed to follow through. I had that kind of macho attitude about it. Rita is one of my old friends, someone I’d known since before the war and talked about these things with. Naturally, it never occurred to me to suspect her.
— You left Russia in December 2025, after a series of administrative arrests. In the interview, Flores talks about it as though she was the one who saved you from a new criminal case supposedly being prepared against you. According to her, it’s only thanks to her that you stayed free and were able to leave. She also says she convinced you to leave Russia by messaging with your wife. Who actually convinced you to leave, and did Rita play any part in that?
— FSB officers came to see me at the holding facility and convinced me, telling me straight out: either I leave, or they lock me up.
They took me into a dark room, stood me facing the wall, and the FSB officers practically read off a script about what a bad person I was, saying they’d lock me up, along with all my relatives, and so on, if I didn’t leave. Only then did something click [in my head] that I really needed to go.
When I got out of the holding facility, my wife and I had a serious talk. She’s the one who finally convinced me.
— What’s your overall impression of what Rita said? Is it possible she embellished parts of her account?
— Oh, I think it’s all of that at once. There’s embellishment, and there’s also this [put-on] air from Rita, like she understood everything while the rest of us didn’t.
I only came to understand that I needed to leave the country after a direct message from FSB officers. Every time I was detained, I said: I’m staying in Russia; if you want me to leave, just tell me straight out, “Leave.” And I will. Because obviously, I wasn’t planning to go to prison a second time.
Both the Center for Combating Extremism and the FSB sensed they had that leverage — that I was a convicted man — and knew they could pressure me.
— Does it bother you that your departure from Russia looked somewhat different from how Rita describes it?
— I think she saw it her own way, and over time it took on different shapes in her memory. [Rita Flores’s] interview can’t be a 100% accurate historical record. We’ll probably never really know how it actually happened.
More than six months have passed [since I left Russia], and for me it already feels like some kind of fictional world. It’s hard to imagine how it really was: the pressure, the surveillance, the detention.
For some reason I’m sure [Rita’s] subconscious hid or reworked a lot of it so she wouldn’t completely lose her mind.
What I saw is that I was detained in Istra at the missile, and I hadn’t told anyone about the performance except the journalists who were with me at the time and Rita. Everything spun out from that detention. Maybe she really did [tell the FSB]… We still can’t fully trust her after something like this. Even though I’m trying to overcome that stigmatization in myself.
— In pretrial detention centers and penal colonies, there are usually people who cooperate with the administration. In exchange for privileges, they inform on others and push fellow convicts to cooperate as well. Did you encounter anything like that while serving your sentence in the hooliganism case?
— Of course I saw all of it — I [did time] with all those bitches who ran to the operations unit. In every cell, every barrack, there’s always someone who cooperates with the administration and snitches on everything that happens.
At Penal Colony No. 5 in Metallostroy, in Russia’s Leningrad region, there was an incident. For most of my time there I didn’t work, because the sewing shop where I’d started out and learned to sew had closed down. We also had a fish-processing shop. I was brought to the operations unit. The operations officer said, “You’re assigned to the fish shop, that’s not up for discussion.” I told him, “Fine, I won’t argue.”
But I didn’t want to spend my last two months working in the fish shop — I didn’t want to stink right before my release. I went back to the barracks and started telling everyone that if they sent me to the fish shop, I’d cut myself, that I had allergies, that sort of thing. In the end, of everyone on the list, I was the only one they didn’t send to the fish shop [Krisevich suspects this happened after other inmates reported his remarks to the colony administration].
— After you were released, did you suspect that people around you might be informing too? Did three and a half years in the colony leave you more cautious, more suspicious?
— Only toward people I didn’t know. Rita and I had known each other a long time.
Now my prison instincts kick in, telling me that Rita is, crudely speaking, marked as a “bitch” [prison slang for an informer]. But I still have human feelings, too.
Rita went through a lot to escape Russia, ended up free, told this whole story, and is trying to help other people who are also entangled with the FSB… She shouldn’t be stigmatized. You have to feel for the person. Because we’re not to blame for having lived in a vile system that literally breaks people to make its future crimes possible.
— Were you surprised that FSB officers took such an interest in the art scene — that they planted agents there, that they recruited Rita?
— Hell if I know. I think there are some ancient prejudices in the security apparatus. An artist is considered a lunatic, someone who can’t be controlled. For people who try to control everything, to keep everything in their own hands, an artist with strange ideas is the main enemy.
It probably also played a part that [Pyotr] Verzilov went off to fight on Ukraine’s side. They think all of us are future militants of that kind.
For most artists, the principle of nonviolence and the principle of conveying their worldview through art come first. Very few would ever take up arms.
It’s a single step, in some sense, from an art performance to blowing up a lawmaker. But I’m sure artists won’t go down that road. And at a time when the FSB should be fighting real terrorists, catching whoever attacked the Crocus City Hall concert venue, it was recruiting Rita Flores.
And now, in Paris, they’re watching me and leaking data of some kind. They’re watching other artists, carrying out the killing of [artist Semyon] Skrepetsky. At a time when they should be fighting real terrorists. But they won’t do that. It’s easier to hit their numbers with artists who won’t fight back. In the physical sense, I mean.
— You’re saying you’re being watched in Paris?
— Rita says there’s someone in my circle running an operation on me.
— Is this something she told you now, after the interview with the outlet Port?
— Yes. Well, I wrote to her that I understand the whole situation, that I forgive her for this first transgression. That the country is vile and can do whatever it wants with a person’s fate if the system decides to. It’s built for that — to break people into whatever shape it needs.
Of course, [thanks to Flores] it was in some ways easier for FSB officers to keep tabs on me. And that may be part of why I ended up emigrating from Russia. What Rita did to other people is on her conscience. It will stay with her, and it will weigh on her too.
— Do you think that now, after this interview, after what Rita told you about the surveillance, artists will be more anxious? Will there be a wave of spy mania?
— I think all artists tensed up the moment Skrepetsky was killed. Though it’s clear the bigger factor there was the Chechen angle and his blunt remarks about Ramzan Kadyrov — that’s a more sensitive topic.
Still, I think everyone will tense up even more now. And that’s also the state’s goal: to keep everyone on edge, to burn people out faster. To drive people into depression with the feeling that “enemies are everywhere, you can’t trust anyone.”
But somehow I keep believing in people… even after all this. And of course I understand that if the state wants to, it will kill me too: poison me, hit me over the back of the head with something heavy while I’m walking through Paris. Because those are the only methods Putin’s state has left. It has no other way to exert influence. Its soft power is gone.
There’s no way to portray us, the artists, as fringe figures in Europe, even after what Pyotr Pavlensky did there.
I’m going to keep going. If I gave up on everything, that would suit Vladimir Vladimirovich just fine. And I want Vladimir Vladimirovich… well, actually, not even him — he doesn’t give a shit, none of this reaches him — I want some security official with stars on his shoulders, maybe some colonel, to be the one who tenses up. To think: there’s Krisevich, still out there saying things, even in Paris.
And maybe get through to the French that [Russia] is a completely sick country. That it does the kinds of things it did to Rita and to me — this exile from Russia — and the things it does to other artists and public figures who disagree with the authorities, don’t want war, and don’t want to live in an authoritarian state with no place for human rights.
— Will you keep in touch with Rita now?
— We exchanged some messages, tried to clear up a few questions. I’ll definitely need to talk to her in person again.
Even after statements like that, after everything that’s happened, we need to talk in person. I want to understand her position fully, now that she’s someone who isn’t locked up, whose passport hasn’t been confiscated, and who isn’t facing the threat of a criminal case or constant FSB pressure. I’ll just meet up with her — if the chance comes up — and talk. But that probably won’t happen soon.
— Do you stay in touch with Philippenzo (Filipp Kozlov), whom Flores was also ordered to inform on?
— We’ve crossed paths a few times. We message occasionally, discuss ideas for street art.
— And now, after Rita’s interview?
— We had a joking exchange, something like: “You seem awfully suspicious. Why are you asking so many questions?”

articles.title: WSJ learns likely reason for CIA director’s visit to Moscow
articles.body:
WSJ learns likely reason for CIA director’s visit to Moscow
                                        
                            
                        —
                25 August, 21:04
                
                                        CIA Director John Ratcliffe. Photo: Getty Images
                                    
                                                        CIA Director John Ratcliffe travelled to Russia because US intelligence had gathered information indicating that Moscow was making early preparations for a possible military mobilisation.
Source: European Pravda, citing The Wall Street Journal
Details: WSJ reported that the US had collected intelligence showing that Russia was making early preparations for a possible military mobilisation for its war against Ukraine and had plans to test NATO's resolve.
Advertisement:
Analysts have suggested that Ratcliffe may have met with Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin to deliver a warning.
Background:
- CBS was the first media outlet to report Ratcliffe's visit. Reports of his visit emerged after a US Air Force Boeing C-17A Globemaster III transport plane and a US diplomatic motorcade were spotted at a Moscow airport.
- The US asked Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russia during the US delegation's visit.
- The last time a CIA director visited Russia in person was in November 2021, when William Burns travelled to Moscow to warn the Kremlin at the highest level that the US was aware of its preparations for a large-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Ads appear in the Moscow metro promising ‘alternative service’ with no front-line deployment. Recruits still sign standard military contracts.
articles.body:
Ads appear in the Moscow metro promising ‘alternative service’ with no front-line deployment. Recruits still sign standard military contracts.
Advertisements for “alternative civilian service” have begun appearing near Moscow metro stations, the independent Russian news outlet Vot Tak reported, citing a reader who spotted the signs.
The human rights project Get Lost had already reported on August 17 that stands advertising alternative service appeared in the Moscow metro.
Vot Tak published a photo of the advertisement, which describes the service as including a one-time payment of 2.3 million rubles, a 5/2 work schedule, benefits, and exemption from mandatory conscription, and rules out deployment to a combat zone. The position is based in Naro-Fominsk, in the Moscow region.
The advertisements seek communications specialists, telecommunications engineers, IT specialists, and drivers. The organization Zashchitnik.rf placed the stands and ads in the metro; according to Vot Tak, it has actively promoted its services on social media since December 2024, acting as an intermediary for people signing contracts with the Defense Ministry.
A Vot Tak correspondent called the number listed in the brochure, posing as a prospective candidate. A Zashchitnik.rf representative said enrolling in alternative service requires signing a standard military contract. Asked whether that person could later be sent to the front, the representative said, “No, that can’t happen.”
Get Lost has said Russians have previously been lured into signing contracts disguised as alternative service. “If you’re told it’s “alternative service by contract,” “one-year service,” “training near Moscow,” “drones,” “air defense,” “computer work,” “not the front,” or a “3/3 schedule” — and you’re handed a contract to sign, that’s not AGS. […] AGS is never arranged through a contract with the Defense Ministry, a volunteer unit, BARS, or any other military structure,” the project wrote.
Alternative civilian service, known as AGS, is work performed “in the interests of society and the state” in place of mandatory military service. The Russian Constitution guarantees it to people whose beliefs or religion conflict with military service, as well as to some members of indigenous peoples with small populations.

articles.title: Why was China’s response to North Korea’s latest missile launches so muted?
articles.body:
Advertisement
Why was China’s response to North Korea’s latest missile launches so muted?
Missile tests hours after China’s foreign minister left Seoul won’t alter Beijing’s focus on regime stability, analysts say
2-MIN READ2-MIN
5
 Listen
China’s muted response to North Korea’s latest missile launch, which came soon after top diplomat Wang Yi’s visit to Seoul, underscores how Beijing is prioritising Pyongyang’s stability over near‑term denuclearisation, according to analysts.
North Korea started launching more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles just hours after Wang concluded his two-day visit on Thursday, the foreign minister’s first official trip to South Korea in nearly five years.
South Korea and Japan condemned the launch as a provocation.
Beijing declined to criticise the barrage fired into the sea east of the peninsula, with China’s foreign ministry saying the following day that it had “noted the reports” and did not have any “new comment”.
The launch highlighted the gap between Beijing’s diplomatic engagement with both Koreas and its ability, or willingness, to restrain North Korea, said Lee Seong‑hyon, a senior fellow at George H.W. Bush Foundation for US-China Relations.
During his meetings in Seoul, Wang urged South Korea to pursue “genuine strategic autonomy”, avoid taking sides between China and the United States and move towards “peaceful coexistence” with its northern neighbour.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Deep Inside Russia Despite Starlink Limits
articles.body:
Ukraine has carried out a series of strikes using FP-2 attack drones against Russian military targets deep inside Russia, including radar stations and facilities in Rostov Oblast, raising questions over how the drones maintain connectivity in areas where Starlink cannot be used, according to Russian and Western OSINT analysts on Tuesday, Aug. 25.
The Russian Telegram channel Military Informant reported strikes against several radar stations and the Kamensky industrial plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov Oblast.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It also reported that drones targeted Russia’s Millerovo airbase, hitting what appeared to be a decoy Ka-52 helicopter and another MiG-29 aircraft that the channel said was likely also being used as a decoy.
The channel noted that Rostov Oblast is not a coastal region and argued that the strikes could therefore not be explained by Ukrainian drones operating through Starlink connectivity.
“Either Starlink’s operation is gradually spreading deep into Russian territory and the US is giving Ukraine the green light for such strikes, or the Ukrainian Armed Forces are using a similar network of repeaters and controlling their drones through a mesh network,” the channel said.
French OSINT analyst Clément Molin similarly highlighted the significance of the strikes, saying that Ukraine was expanding its use of medium-range drones with video feeds deeper into Russian territory.
Kanye West’s Russia Concerts in Limbo After St. Petersburg Arena Pulls Out
Molin said dozens of Ukrainian strikes in 2026 had targeted Russian air-defense systems, radars and aircraft, with more than 250 such assets reportedly damaged or destroyed this year, including air-defense systems, jammers and radars.
How Ukraine could control drones beyond Starlink coverage
According to Molin, Starlink connectivity allows Ukrainian FP-2 drones to operate across occupied Ukrainian territory, the Black Sea and coastal areas of Russia.
However, he said the recent footage from strikes against Russian airbases and air-defense systems was significant because Starlink reportedly cannot be used at those locations.
Molin suggested that Ukraine could be using a mesh network with repeater drones to maintain communications with the attacking drones over longer distances.
A mesh network would allow drones or other relay devices to pass communications between each other, potentially extending the range at which operators can maintain contact with a drone.
The analysts did not provide evidence confirming that Ukraine is using such a system in these specific attacks.
Strikes could open gaps in Russia’s defenses
Molin said the destruction of Russian radars and air-defense systems could create new vulnerabilities along Russia’s southern border.
He argued that this could eventually allow Ukraine to conduct longer-range strikes against Russian energy infrastructure and industrial facilities in areas including Voronezh, Rostov and Krasnodar.
The strikes could also potentially affect Russian missile systems positioned close to Ukraine, including Iskander and S-400 launchers in Bryansk, Kursk and Belgorod oblasts that are used to attack Ukrainian targets.
The analysts’ assessments remain preliminary, and the precise communications technology used to control the drones in these strikes has not been independently established.

articles.title: Gambler’s hand revealed to Iran
articles.body:
Gambler’s hand revealed to Iran
Trump plays the economic war card with Bessent while sending Field Marshal Asim Munir to seek a face-saving exit from the quagmire of war with Iran
TEHRAN — Pakistan’s Chief of Defense Forces, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi wrapped up a day-long official visit to Tehran on Monday night after holding talks with senior Iranian political and security leadership aimed at advancing a comprehensive framework for resolving regional issues.
“Our discussion focused on the Iran-US conflict, tensions in the Middle East, the way forward, and the steps needed by both sides for the restoration of the Islamabad MoU,” Naqvi said in a post on X, referring to the Pakistani-mediated memorandum of understanding that President Donald Trump signed with Iran on June 17.
Naqvi added, “The Iranian President candidly shared his government’s perspective and concerns, and we had a very constructive exchange on the issues involved. Significant progress was made, and the meeting concluded on a highly positive note.”
The Pakistani-mediated MoU established framework terms to cease hostilities between Iran and the US. While subsequent US aerial strikes and naval blockades disrupted the agreement, Pakistan had already demonstrated its diplomatic role by helping facilitate the April 8 ceasefire that paused the 39-day war that the US and Israel launched on Iran on February 28.
The Pakistani delegation held comprehensive discussions with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) Secretary Mohsen Rezaei, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni. Pakistan says the Iranian leadership highly appreciated Islamabad’s constructive role and sincere efforts in facilitating dialogue and de-escalation.
Seyed Mehdi Tabatabaei, deputy for communications and information at the Iranian President’s Office, also described Munir’s trip as “highly productive.”
“Contrary to some inaccurate media speculation, the visit of Field Marshal Asim Munir, the army chief of friendly Pakistan, to Iran was highly productive and yielded significant diplomatic achievements, the results of which will become apparent soon,” Tabatabaei wrote on X.
In a meeting with the Pakistan delegation, President Pezeshkian stated that the United States must abandon its reliance on force and bullying, warning that such an approach will only complicate efforts to implement the MoU and resolve regional issues.
“The United States must correct its tone and approach in interacting with Iran,” the president said. “Relying on coercion and bullying will only make the implementation process more complicated.”
Pezeshkian highlighted the Iranian nation’s resilience and steadfastness, attributing it to national unity and cohesion. “Drawing on this solidarity, our nation will overcome any pressure or threat,” he stated.
Pezeshkian also hoped that Islamabad’s diplomatic efforts would contribute to the growing prosperity, dignity, and pride of the region and the wider Islamic world.
Field Marshal Munir, for his part, thanked President Pezeshkian for his efforts to foster stability and calm in the region. He stressed that diplomatic processes must be examined with the utmost precision and care to advance shared goals and reach a comprehensive agreement.
He said cultural commonalities between Iran and Pakistan represent a valuable asset for overcoming current complex conditions and charting a bright future.
During a separate meeting with Field Marshal Munir, the secretary of SNSC said Iran remains distrustful of the United States. Washington, he added, must take practical steps to implement the provisions of the Pakistan-brokered MoU.
Iran’s Parliament speaker also pointed to the US failure to honor its commitments under the memorandum of understanding as he held talks with the visiting Pakistani delegation.
“The commitments made by both sides under the memorandum of understanding are clear. It was the United States’ failure to honor its commitments that undermined regional stability and gave us yet another reason not to trust Washington,” Qalibaf told Asim Munir. The top Pakistani military official, for his part, reiterated that he would continue efforts to help restore regional peace.
The US escalates economic war
While backchannel diplomatic efforts unfolded in Tehran, the Trump administration on Monday announced a parallel plan to isolate Iran’s economy by threatening to impose secondary sanctions on countries supporting Iran.
“We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said as he unveiled the new sanctions scheme, dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast.”
Trump is calling world leaders and making “specific requests to cease their interactions” with Iran, Bessent said at the Treasury Department.
“Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.”
Bessent suggested at Monday’s event that China would not be exempt.
“We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions,” Bessent said when asked if the administration would target Chinese banks, or if it would avoid doing so in order to preserve relations with Beijing. “If they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”
In response, China vowed to protect its interests. Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.
Lin added: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."
Qatar also described US sanctions on Iran as unilateral and reiterated its firm backing for mediation efforts to bridge the divide between the two sides.
Taken together, these developments expose the growing contradictions at the heart of Trump’s Iran policy. On the one hand, Trump is sending Bessent to press ahead with yet another round of economic warfare against Iran, threatening countries and financial institutions that continue to maintain legitimate economic ties with Tehran. On the other hand, Washington is turning to Pakistan’s top military leadership to help persuade Iran to revive a diplomatic process that could pull the United States out of the quagmire created by its failed war.
The contradiction could hardly be more striking.
While Bessent announced what the Trump administration calls “Operation Economic Outcast,” threatening secondary sanctions against countries and entities dealing with Iran, Asim Munir was in Tehran holding high-level talks with Iran’s political and security leadership. It appears that his mission was not to deliver another threat from Washington, but to help revive a diplomatic framework that the United States itself failed to honor.
That contrast lays bare the limits of Trump’s approach. Washington is simultaneously escalating pressure on Tehran and seeking a diplomatic channel through Islamabad to address the very crisis that its own military and economic policies have deepened.
Iran, however, made clear that diplomacy cannot succeed through pressure and intimidation. In other words, Tehran is not closing the door to diplomacy. It is demanding that Washington stop trying to force its way through that door.
Amid the US failure in the war on Iran, the pattern is becoming increasingly clear. Washington continues to reach for the same instruments—military pressure, sanctions, threats and economic coercion—while simultaneously searching for intermediaries capable of creating an exit from the confrontation.
Trump therefore finds himself caught between two contradictory impulses: escalating the pressure in the hope of forcing Iran into submission, while seeking mediation to prevent the confrontation from spiraling further.
That is the behavior of a gambler who keeps doubling down after a series of losses, hoping that the next move will reverse his fortunes.
But Iran’s resilience, the failure of military pressure to produce capitulation, the continued resistance to economic coercion and the growing willingness of regional actors to pursue diplomacy have made Washington’s predicament increasingly difficult to conceal.
Trump may continue to raise the stakes, but the more he does so, the clearer the contradictions become. One hand is pushing sanctions and threats; the other is reaching for diplomacy through Islamabad.
Ultimately, the US president is acting like a desperate gambler trying to recover his losses by placing yet another bet. But this time, there is little left to conceal: the losing gambler’s cards are now fully exposed on the table.

articles.title: Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery Halts Operations After Overnight Drone Attack
articles.body:
The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in Rostov region, Russia, has suspended operations following a UAV attack last night.
Yuriy Slyusar, the region’s governor, reported this on Telegram.
Eyewitnesses among the local residents filmed the sounds of drones flying overhead, the operation of Russian air defenses, and explosions in the plant’s area.
“According to updated information, the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery was damaged in an overnight enemy attack on the Rostov region. The facility has temporarily suspended operations,” the Russian official said.
The Novoshakhtinsk refinery’s design capacity is estimated at approximately 7.5 million tonnes of crude oil per year (equivalent to around 112,000–115,000 barrels per day), although some sources cite figures ranging from 5.6 to 7.5 million tonnes per year, depending on the estimate.
The plant began operations in 2009. It became one of the first large oil refineries built in Russia in a long time.
The refinery is connected to main oil pipelines via the Transneft system, as well as rail lines, ensuring crude oil supply and shipping finished products by rail and water via a terminal on the Don River.
The facility has been attacked repeatedly in the past. In particular, during the night of May 31 this year, a strike with Neptune cruise missiles knocked two oil-processing units out of service.
Without these facilities, further oil refining is practically impossible, as they constitute the first stage of the entire refinery production cycle.
The Navy noted that the refinery is a key facility in Russia’s regional fuel infrastructure and plays an important role in supplying the occupation forces with fuel and lubricants.
In addition, on December 25, 2025, Ukrainian Air Force aircraft struck the Russian refinery with Storm Shadow cruise missiles. The strike caused a major fire at the facility.
Ukrainian drones also struck the Afipsky Oil Refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai on the night of August 25, causing a fire at the facility.
