articles.title: US-led Gaza peace board warns Hamas over kites after Israeli threat
articles.body:
US-led Gaza peace board warns Hamas over kites after Israeli threat
The US-led board overseeing the Gaza peace plan warned Hamas on Tuesday to halt militant activity, including flying kites, after Israel threatened retaliatory strikes. A Board of Peace official said Israel must also respect the ceasefire, limiting military action to responses to “genuine and imminent threats.”
The US-led board supervising a Gaza peace plan on Tuesday warned Hamas against flying kites, after Israel threatened retaliatory strikes.
"All militant activity in Gaza must stop, including the flying of kites. We have conveyed this message directly through the established mechanism," an official on President Donald Trump's "Board of Peace" said on condition of anonymity.
"Israel, too, must comply with the ceasefire. Military action cannot extend beyond responding to genuine and imminent threats," the official said.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday warned Hamas that Israel would step up operations in Gaza if it launches kites, drones or balloons.
Read moreTrump's Board of Peace reassures Israel after objections on Gaza pullout plan
The threat came after a series of kites reportedly were found across the Gaza border in southern Israel, communities traumatised by the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023.
The episode revived memories of incendiary kites and balloons once launched from Gaza. The latest kites are not known to have had any explosives, although Israeli media reported at least one with a political message.
Hamas political bureau member Basem Naim voiced outrage at the warning on kites conveyed via the Board of Peace.
"What audacity! Is it conceivable that attempts to appease the war criminal Netanyahu have led them to describe innocent children's activities as armed activities, while Netanyahu continues to kill and destroy daily despite the agreement?"
The United Nations earlier Tuesday described the Israeli threats over the kites as unacceptable.
"On the threat of expulsion due to children's kite flying, I hope we can all agree that this is outrageous," UN rights office spokeswoman Ravina Shamdasani told reporters in Geneva.
Read moreWhat we know about the Hamas disarmament deal announced by Trump
The Board of Peace was put in place by Trump to oversee a ceasefire declared in October in the bloody conflict in Gaza.
Since then, Israel has expanded slightly further into Gaza and kept up strikes, which have killed 1,288 Palestinians, according to health authorities under Hamas whose figures are generally considered reliable by the UN.
On Monday, Gaza authorities said Israeli fire killed at least five people including two children.
Netanyahu, facing tight elections in October, earlier this month rejected the latest stage in the Gaza peace plan after Hamas said it had agreed to disarm.
Netanyahu voiced scepticism over the promises and told Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner last week that a US general should be placed in charge of verifying the destruction of all Hamas's weapons.
In response to Netanyahu, the Board of Peace backtracked and assured him that Israeli troops need not leave Gaza until a complete demilitarisation of Hamas. Earlier the board had called for Israel to start a phased withdrawal.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Strategic vacuum: Why is Trump's economic warfare against Iran doomed to fail?
articles.body:
Strategic vacuum: Why is Trump's economic warfare against Iran doomed to fail?
TEHRAN- Six months into his military campaign against Iran, Donald Trump finds himself trapped in the very quagmire he promised to eliminate. What began as a boastful declaration of "decisive action" to crush Iran and effect regime change has devolved into a strategic fiasco that not only fails to achieve its objectives but is inflicting profound damage on the U.S. economy and global stability. The administration's latest gambit—announcing the "largest financial attack in history" against Iran on August 24, a self-styled "D-Day" of economic warfare—appears less a stroke of genius and more an act of desperation from a presidency with no viable strategy left.
The irony is palpable. As U.S. Treasury officials threaten economic Armageddon against Tehran, America's own energy reserves are collapsing. Official data from July 2026 reveals that U.S. crude oil stockpiles, including the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), have plummeted to their lowest level in half a century—just 41 days of coverage, compared to the historical average of 65 days. Washington has depleted its most powerful tool for market intervention, leaving itself exposed to any future supply shock. This is not strength; this is strategic bankruptcy disguised as aggression.
The root cause of this self-inflicted wound lies in the Strait of Hormuz, the world's most vital energy chokepoint. After nearly six months of severe disruption triggered by the U.S.-Israeli military aggression against Iran, the waterway that once carried one-fifth of global oil and LNG supply has been reduced to a fraction of its normal flow. Daily transits have plummeted from 130 vessels to just a few, and war-risk insurance premiums have soared to 40 times normal levels. Hundreds of ships remain trapped in the Persian Gulf, and global oil flows have collapsed from 21 million barrels per day to a trickle. Iran, facing a U.S. naval blockade, has responded with controlled restrictions on the strait, creating a standoff that punishes everyone.
The economic devastation is global in scope. Asia, which historically received 80 to 90 percent of Hormuz-shipped oil and LNG, is enduring its largest energy shock in history. Japan, South Korea, India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh face crippling fuel shortages, soaring inflation, and industrial paralysis. European nations grapple with surging gas and electricity prices, while African countries dependent on food and energy imports confront acute shortages. The World Bank and institutions like Wood Mackenzie and Capital Economics warn that prolonged disruption could shave 0.5 to 1 percent off global GDP growth—a staggering blow to an already fragile world economy.
But perhaps the most telling consequence is the blowback on the United States itself. Trump's "maximum pressure" campaign has not broken Iran; it has made the regime more resilient. Airstrikes have weakened Iran militarily but strengthened its internal cohesion. The war has destroyed Iranian infrastructure and claimed lives, yet for most Americans, the conflict remains a distant abstraction—except at the gas pump, where prices have surged, and in the inflationary pressures now spreading through the U.S. economy. The SPR depletion is not a sign of American might; it is a warning that Washington has overextended itself and lost its ability to respond to future crises.
Trump's strategy rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of Iran. The Islamic Republic is simultaneously ideological and pragmatic. It resisted U.S. pressure for decades; it will not capitulate to coercion. Instead, by controlling the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran has demonstrated that it can impose reciprocal costs on its adversaries—and those costs are now painfully evident.
The administration's D-Day economic offensive is not a game-changer; it is a last gasp. Trump has repeated the same flawed playbook that has failed U.S. presidents since 1979: pressure as a substitute for strategy, military bluster as a cover for diplomatic bankruptcy. But this time, the consequences are not confined to Iran. The global economy is reeling, U.S. strategic reserves are depleted, and America's credibility is eroding with every empty threat. Far from breaking Iran, Trump's war has exposed the limits of American power and inflicted greater harm on the United States and its allies than on the intended target. The red light is flashing—not for Tehran, but for Washington.

articles.title: CIA director John Ratcliffe reportedly on Moscow visit
articles.body:
The CIA director, John Ratcliffe, has made an unannounced visit to Moscow, US media reported, after flight data showed an American military aircraft flew to the Russian capital, where a US diplomatic motorcade was later spotted.
CBS News quoted sources familiar with the situation as confirming Ratcliffe’s trip, saying it was his first known visit to Russia as CIA chief. Axios separately confirmed the visit, quoting a US official.
The Financial Times reported that the Trump administration had asked Kyiv to pause its long-range strikes on major Russian cities during the course of the visit.
There was no immediate comment from the CIA or the White House.
Data from Flightradar24 showed a US military C-17 travelling from the US to Latvia and then on to Moscow. The tracker showed that the flight originated from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, best known for hosting Air Force One.
The C-17 Globemaster III is a large military transport aircraft that the US air force website says can be used for strategic and tactical airlift and airdrop missions as well as aeromedical evacuations.
Ratcliffe’s reported visit comes as US-brokered talks aimed at ending Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have stalled. However, earlier this month Moscow freed a former US marine detained since 2022, amid concerns about his health.
The reason for the visit is unclear but the CIA has mediated in recent US-Russia detainee exchanges and was involved in the 2024 prisoner exchange that secured the release of the Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich and the marine veteran Paul Whelan.
Some speculation has focused on the war in Iran, which remains a bone of contention between Moscow and Washington. On Monday the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced a new economic sanctions strategy designed to isolate Iran.

articles.title: Burnham plans a trip to the US to persuade Trump to strengthen Ukraine’s air defense
articles.body:
Burnham plans a trip to the US to persuade Trump to strengthen Ukraine’s air defense
Kyiv • UNN
The British prime minister plans to meet with Trump in the US in September. He wants to negotiate additional Patriot missiles for Ukraine.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham plans to visit the United States in September and discuss with President Donald Trump the transfer of additional Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine before winter. Burnham said this in an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv, UNN reports.
Details
Burnham said he intends to travel to New York for a session of the UN General Assembly. This will be his first visit to the United States since being appointed prime minister.
I am looking forward to travelling to New York in September
According to him, following the talks in Kyiv, he has a clear understanding of what needs to be done over the coming weeks.
Europe wants additional Patriot missiles
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly called on the United States and European countries to help with Patriot interceptor missiles and replenish their stocks before winter. During the cold season, Russia is expected to intensify strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
British Prime Minister Burnham visited wounded soldiers in Kyiv24.08.26, 23:27 • 1296 views
Burnham said European leaders were considering holding another meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in New York. According to him, the aim could be to provide Ukraine with American interceptor missiles and supplies from other countries.
There are other players who could help with this issue, over whom we have influence
At the same time, Trump previously backed away from an earlier promise to provide or allow Ukraine to produce interceptor missiles for Patriot systems. Burnham said that Ukraine's current problems with an insufficient number of missiles to defend against Russian ballistic strikes could be resolved.

articles.title: Zelenskyy comments on possible support from Ukraine in event of Russian attack on Baltic states
articles.body:
Zelenskyy comments on possible support from Ukraine in event of Russian attack on Baltic states
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has commented on the possibility of helping the Baltic states in the event of a potential Russian attack on them.
Source: Ukrainian news agency Ukrinform citing Zelenskyy during a joint press conference with his Estonian counterpart Alar Karis in Kyiv, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Asked whether Ukraine would send its troops in the event of an attack on Estonia, Zelenskyy said the Baltic states should be protected by NATO.
Quote: "As for our military, Ukraine is not in NATO. Estonia is in NATO. If we believe in the strength of NATO, then Estonia – God forbid, but if there are any risks – has more than 30 countries that, in my view, should simultaneously defend any country that is a NATO ally."
Background:
- Earlier, Reuters reported that Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are cooperating to shield their infrastructure from potential Russian attacks that could be staged as false-flag operations, as allied intelligence services have repeatedly warned.
- Last month, Lithuania deployed troops to reinforce special forces in order to secure its liquefied natural gas import terminal, oil products terminal, a key power line with Poland and the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydroelectric Plant.
- Leaders of NATO's eastern flank countries have recently issued public warnings, citing intelligence indicating that Russia is preparing provocations on their territory.
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: CIA chief was aboard mystery US C-17 flight to Moscow
articles.body:
We now know why a US Air Force C-17 made an unusual flight from Riga to Moscow: CIA Director John Ratcliffe was aboard the aircraft for meetings in the Russian capital.
The reason behind an unusual US Air Force C-17 Globemaster III flight into Moscow has now emerged, with CBS News reporting that CIA Director John Ratcliffe travelled aboard the aircraft for meetings in the Russian capital, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The development answers the central question raised when the aircraft appeared on civilian flight-tracking services earlier on 25 August. What initially looked like a highly unusual American military transport movement into Russia was, according to CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, carrying the CIA Director on a visit to Moscow. Jacobs reported, citing sources, that Ratcliffe travelled to Russia aboard a C-17 for meetings in the city and said it appeared to be his first known trip to the country since becoming CIA Director, although he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts.
It appears to be Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Russia as CIA director, though he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts. https://t.co/J9ugJvGnSj
— Jennifer Jacobs (@JenniferJJacobs) August 25, 2026
The aircraft was identified through open-source flight data as US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III serial 07-7191, using the callsign REACH 4555. It had first been tracked leaving the Washington area for Riga on 23 August, before departing the Latvian capital two days later and heading east towards Moscow, a routing that immediately drew attention because direct movements by identifiable US military aircraft into Russia have become extremely uncommon amid the deterioration in relations between Washington and Moscow.
UK Defence Journal Senior Editor Jon, known as DefenceGeek on X, followed the movement as it developed, first noting the aircraft’s arrival in Riga and then its subsequent flight into Russia. Tracking data showed REACH 4555 approaching Moscow before video and photographs from the city showed a C-17 descending towards the Russian capital, confirming that the aircraft had completed the unusual journey.
At that stage, however, the aircraft itself offered little indication of what the mission involved. The C-17 is the US Air Force’s principal heavy strategic transport aircraft and is routinely used to move personnel, vehicles and outsized cargo over intercontinental distances, while REACH callsigns are commonly associated with US Air Mobility Command missions, meaning the route could be followed in public without revealing who was aboard or why the aircraft had been sent to Moscow.
The CBS reporting changes that picture considerably, placing the flight in the context of a senior US intelligence visit rather than an unexplained logistics movement. Ratcliffe’s reported presence also helps explain why a conspicuous military aircraft was being used on a route that would otherwise have appeared highly unusual, although the precise purpose of his meetings, the Russian officials he met and the subjects discussed have not been made public.
Separate activity around the flight had already suggested that the movement involved more than a routine cargo mission. Imagery circulating after the C-17 arrived appeared to show US government vehicles travelling in convoy through Moscow, with open-source observers pointing to registration plates that appeared consistent with Latvia-issued diplomatic plates. The timing now makes a connection with Ratcliffe’s visit more plausible, although the available imagery does not establish whether those vehicles carried the CIA Director, formed part of his security detail or had any direct connection with the delegation.
There was also additional US government aviation activity at Riga before REACH 4555 continued to Moscow. A Boeing C-40, serial 02-0042 and using the callsign REACH 790, was tracked arriving at Riga International Airport from Joint Base Andrews on 23 August, with open-source imagery suggesting that it was parked close to the C-17. That movement can now be viewed alongside Ratcliffe’s reported journey, but there is still no confirmation that the C-40 continued to Russia or that it played a direct role in the CIA Director’s visit.
Jacobs’ reporting that Ratcliffe has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts is also significant because it indicates that direct intelligence channels between Washington and Moscow have continued despite the wider breakdown in political and military relations. What those contacts have covered remains unknown, and there is no public information establishing whether the Moscow meetings concerned Ukraine, detainees, strategic stability, intelligence liaison or another issue.
The known sequence is now considerably clearer than it was when REACH 4555 first appeared over Russia: the aircraft travelled from the United States to Riga, later flew onward to Moscow, and was subsequently identified by CBS News sources as carrying the CIA Director for meetings in the Russian capital. The reason for the flight is therefore no longer the mystery it was when the movement was first detected, even if the substance of Ratcliffe’s discussions remains undisclosed.
The US Air Force declined to comment when approached about the flight, while no detailed public account of Ratcliffe’s meetings has yet been issued by the CIA or Russian authorities. What remains unanswered is not why an American C-17 was in Moscow, but what brought the CIA Director there and what was discussed once he arrived.

The C-17 is the US Air Force’s principal heavy strategic transport aircraft and is routinely used to move personnel, vehicles and outsized cargo over intercontinental distances, while REACH callsigns are commonly associated with US Air Mobility Command missions, meaning the route could be followed in public without revealing who was aboard or why the aircraft had been sent to Moscow.
The CBS reporting changes that picture considerably, placing the flight in the context of a senior US intelligence visit rather than an unexplained logistics movement. Ratcliffe’s reported presence also helps explain why a conspicuous military aircraft was being used on a route that would otherwise have appeared highly unusual, although the precise purpose of his meetings, the Russian officials he met and the subjects discussed have not been made public.
Separate activity around the flight had already suggested that the movement involved more than a routine cargo mission. Imagery circulating after the C-17 arrived appeared to show US government vehicles travelling in convoy through Moscow, with open-source observers pointing to registration plates that appeared consistent with Latvia-issued diplomatic plates. The timing now makes a connection with Ratcliffe’s visit more plausible, although the available imagery does not establish whether those vehicles carried the CIA Director, formed part of his security detail or had any direct connection with the delegation.
There was also additional US government aviation activity at Riga before REACH 4555 continued to Moscow. A Boeing C-40, serial 02-0042 and using the callsign REACH 790, was tracked arriving at Riga International Airport from Joint Base Andrews on 23 August, with open-source imagery suggesting that it was parked close to the C-17. That movement can now be viewed alongside Ratcliffe’s reported journey, but there is still no confirmation that the C-40 continued to Russia or that it played a direct role in the CIA Director’s visit.
Jacobs’ reporting that Ratcliffe has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts is also significant because it indicates that direct intelligence channels between Washington and Moscow have continued despite the wider breakdown in political and military relations. What those contacts have covered remains unknown, and there is no public information establishing whether the Moscow meetings concerned Ukraine, detainees, strategic stability, intelligence liaison or another issue.
The known sequence is now considerably clearer than it was when REACH 4555 first appeared over Russia: the aircraft travelled from the United States to Riga, later flew onward to Moscow, and was subsequently identified by CBS News sources as carrying the CIA Director for meetings in the Russian capital. The reason for the flight is therefore no longer the mystery it was when the movement was first detected, even if the substance of Ratcliffe’s discussions remains undisclosed.
The US Air Force declined to comment when approached about the flight, while no detailed public account of Ratcliffe’s meetings has yet been issued by the CIA or Russian authorities. What remains unanswered is not why an American C-17 was in Moscow, but what brought the CIA Director there and what was discussed once he arrived.

articles.title: Uganda's Gaza 'stabilisation force' plan sparks debate in Africa
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Uganda's participation in Gaza 'stabilisation force' sparks debate in Africa
Uganda's parliament approved the deployment of army troops to the" International Stabilisation Force" in the Gaza Strip at the beginning of August as part of US President Donald Trump's plan. The move marks the first official declaration by an African country of its readiness to participate in Gaza.
The approval came on 6 August after Ugandan Defence Minister Kiria Kiwanuka told lawmakers that Trump had asked President Yoweri Museveni in July for Uganda to contribute to the proposed international force in Gaza.
After the Ugandan parliament's approval, a Ugandan soldier in military uniform posted a video on social media in which he appeared alongside the words, "Gaza, we are coming", indicating that the idea of a military deployment had begun circulating within Uganda's military and media circles.
The Ugandan government has not yet specified the number of troops it may deploy to the territory or when they would be sent.
Israel's public broadcaster reported last Monday, 17 August, that senior officers from Uganda and Burundi had arrived at the US command headquarters in Kiryat Gat in the occupied Palestinian territories as part of advanced talks with the two countries to send hundreds of soldiers to the territory as part of the multinational stabilisation force.
The broadcaster also said last Thursday, 20 August, that Morocco had been chosen to train members of the force.
Ugandan forces in the Gaza stabilisation force has sparked debate inside the Ugandan parliament, with opposition lawmakers calling for more information about the nature of the mission, the number of troops, its funding, and the guarantees provided to soldiers and their families.
The opposition also warned of the security and political risks associated with sending troops to a devastated territory and under highly complex field conditions.
Uganda has extensive experience in peacekeeping operations, particularly in Africa, where its forces participate in missions in Somalia, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The defence minister cited this experience to justify the Ugandan army's ability to participate in a new international mission.
Without African backing
The decision has also raised questions about Kampala's approval of it and whether it has broad African backing or bypasses African consensus by being taken without Uganda consulting its partners in the African Union.
The African Union has consistently supported the Palestinian cause in principle and calls for the implementation of a two-state solution.
However, Israel has built relations with several African countries over decades, viewing the continent as an arena of Arab-Israeli competition.
In 2021, the union accepted Israel as an "observer member", a move that prompted Palestinian and Arab protests and was later revoked.
Uganda's relations with Israel, meanwhile, have continued to grow.
The Ugandan judge Julia Sebutinde, vice-president of the International Court of Justice, has attracted attention after she was described as believing that "God relies on her to stand with Israel". Sebutinde opposed the six rulings imposed by the court in 2024 to protect Palestinians and stop the genocide in Gaza.
Ugandan military leadership also recently said that any attempts to "destroy" Israel, amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, could prompt Uganda to intervene in support of the occupying state.
Uganda is also one of the largest importers of military technology and spyware from the occupying state.
In this context, Sudanese writer and researcher Abbas Saleh, who is based in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, told The New Arab that Uganda's potential participation in the proposed international force for the Gaza Strip reflects a renewed predicament facing the African Union.
Decisions and positions adopted by the continental organisation often appear non-binding on member states, which may adopt unilateral policies that conflict with the union's collective positions.
"Despite the clear positions adopted by the African Union on the Palestinian cause, its rejection of Israeli violations and its repeated calls for an end to the war and the protection of civilians, the involvement of some member states in international security arrangements linked to Gaza could weaken the unity of the African position and expose the organisation's limited ability to turn its political positions into practical commitments by its members," he pointed out.
According to Saleh, Uganda is among the countries whose name has for years been associated with a broad security and military role in Africa, as well as close relations with Western powers, particularly in the Great Lakes region and the Horn of Africa.
He explained that this role "has given it a prominent position in several regional security issues but has at times made its foreign policy a subject of debate over the extent to which its decisions are independent of the calculations of international powers".
"The Ugandan move is significant beyond the participation of a single country, as it could set a precedent encouraging other countries that had been hesitant or reluctant to join the proposed international force, particularly if they are provided with appropriate political and security guarantees or international incentives," Saleh opined.
He stressed that participation in a military mission inside Gaza carries significant risks, given the complexities of the security and political situation, continuing disagreements over the future of the territory and governance and security arrangements, and the sensitivity surrounding the presence of foreign forces in the Palestinian territories.
"Uganda's move places the African Union before a difficult test: how can the organisation maintain a unified African position on the Palestinian cause while each member state has broad scope to make its foreign and security decisions independently?" he added. "The union's ability to deal with these contradictions could be an important indicator of the effectiveness of its political positions, not only towards Palestine, but also towards international crises affecting the continent and the interests of its countries."
Contradictions, differences
Meanwhile, researcher on Sahel and Sahara affairs Mohamed Torshin told The New Arab that the participation of Ugandan forces in the peace process in Gaza clearly reflects the scale of contradictions within the African Union and its limited ability to impose or implement decisions taken collectively, whether at the level of the AU Commission, the Peace and Security Council or the General Assembly.
Although African Union decisions and collective positions are supposed to form a common political framework for member states, the Ugandan position, along with other previous cases, reveals clear differences in the positions of African countries towards several sensitive regional and international issues.
In many cases, these differences push some countries or regional blocs to adopt policies and approaches that conflict with the union's collective position.
According to Torshin, the repercussions are not limited to a particular issue but extend to the effectiveness of African decision-making in general.
When a member state, in his view, adopts a position that clearly contradicts the union's collective position, this weakens the organisation's ability to present itself as a unified political actor and limits its ability to exercise diplomatic influence on issues requiring a coherent continental position.
In this context, Torshin noted that the repetition of such cases could widen the gap between decisions issued by African Union institutions and the policies pursued by some member states at the national level.
"This would gradually weaken the ability of the AU Commission and its political bodies to turn collective positions and decisions into effective and binding policies, making African decision-making more vulnerable to fragmentation and differences between countries and regional blocs," he added.
Torshin pointed out that the lack of protocol and political coordination between different African countries, ministries and institutions, and the absence of unified positions and decisions on common issues, could create space for international parties with interests and programmes in Africa to deal with countries individually and implement their policies and projects according to their own interests, away from the collective frameworks and decisions of the African Union.
He argued that "as this divergence and the multiplicity of positions within the continental organisation continue, international powers may find themselves with greater room to manoeuvre and negotiate with African countries bilaterally, gradually weakening the union's ability to formulate and defend a unified African agenda".
"In the long term, the continuation of this fragmentation could affect the future of African integration, making the implementation of continental policies and projects more closely tied to the interests of countries and external partners, and less subject to the collective vision that the union is supposed to represent," Torshin warned.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Third drone and suspected military explosives found near Leipzig airport
articles.body:
German investigators uncovered a third drone and suspected military explosives thought to be connected to an attempted attack on Leipzig airport, local media have reported.
The drone was discovered in Kabelsketal, just to the west of the airport, along with about 50g (1.8oz) of a suspected military explosive on 14 August, 10 days after the unsuccessful sabotage. Leipzig airport is a cargo and military logistics hub used by Nato and Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines for transporting military supplies.
The office of the prosecutor general, which is leading the investigation, declined to comment on Tuesday. But the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said the government would soon provide information about who it believed was behind the drone attacks.
“They will pay for this,” Merz said, stopping short of naming a suspect, before a cabinet meeting in Brandenburg. He added that the government was “working intensively on this together with the security authorities and we will present our findings and comment on them shortly”.
Intelligence sources cited by the broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung said they suspected the involvement of Russian intelligence in the attempted attack. Moscow has denied involvement.
The German government has so far avoided expressing a clear position as to whether it thinks Russia, or an actor close to it, is responsible.
Merz said the attempted attack showed that Germany was increasingly becoming a target. “Attackers are increasingly ruthlessly accepting even serious property damage, and even injuries and deaths,” he said on Tuesday.
A drone carrying explosives was found on 4 August near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used for military supplies. According to investigators, the drone was apparently intended to land on the wings of the aircraft, which was filled with kerosene, but the explosive device did not detonate.
Investigators say that about 20 minutes after the discovery of the first drone, a second drone possibly collided with a DHL cargo plane, which was forced to abort its landing manoeuvre and was diverted to Marseille.
According to the latest media reports, an inspection of the DHL aircraft revealed damage to the tail section, suggesting a collision with an object. However, the drone has not yet been found. Investigators believe it could have been sucked into the engines after the collision and shredded into small pieces.
The third drone was found in a field in a municipality that directly borders the western edge of Leipzig airport. Forensic technicians from the federal criminal police office found residues of a substance that initial assessments indicated could have been the highly explosive substance hexogen. This explosive also failed to detonate, but the investigators’ report, according to the media reports, stated: “The perpetrators may have had a far larger attack in mind than previously known to the public.”
Other suspicious traces and components were also discovered close to the airport, the report said. In Kursdorf, investigators found an antenna attached to a tree, and other electronic parts, which may have been used to control the drones. Close by and near where witnesses reported hearing a loud bang on the day of the incident, investigators discovered a burnt patch and charred metal parts.
If the drones had exploded, they could have caused a catastrophe, German officials said.

articles.title: Israeli airstrike, artillery shelling hit southern Lebanon despite US-mediated deal
articles.body:
Sahin Demir
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Israeli army forces carried out an airstrike and artillery shelling in southern Lebanon early Tuesday, and erected new earth barriers in the area, in the latest violation of a US-mediated framework agreement, Lebanese media reported.
Israeli warplanes struck the course of the Litani River below the Deir Mar Mima monastery in the town of Deir Mimas at around 4 am local time (0100GMT), according to Lebanon’s official National News Agency (NNA).
Separately, the town of Markaba in the Marjayoun district came under Israeli artillery shelling as Israeli military vehicles were seen moving in the town, the agency said.
NNA also reported that Israeli forces stationed in Kfar Kila and Tall al-Nahhas erected an earth barrier at the Deir Mimas-Burj al-Muluk-Kfar Kila junction toward Tall al-Nahhas, around 150 meters (492 feet) from inhabited homes in Burj al-Muluk.
Israeli forces erected another earth barrier at the Deir Mimas-Burj al-Muluk-Houra junction toward the Houra area, it added.
The violations come amid continuing tensions between Israel and Lebanon following the outbreak of a new round of hostilities on March 2.
Israel has launched extensive attacks on Lebanon since March 2, claiming they targeted Hezbollah, while the group responded with attacks against Israel, effectively ending the ceasefire that had been in place since November 2024.
US-led diplomatic efforts led to the signing of a framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon in June, which provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from all occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army there and the disarmament of armed groups.

articles.title: US targets 1,000-plus Tomahawks a year
articles.body:
Raytheon has received a seven-year contract worth $22.9 billion to sharply increase Tomahawk cruise missile production, with annual output planned to rise above 1,000 weapons for the US Navy and allied customers.
The United States is moving to raise annual production of Tomahawk long-range cruise missiles to more than 1,000 weapons under a seven-year contract awarded to Raytheon, according to the company.
The RTX news update values the agreement at $22.9 billion, approximately £16.8 billion, and says it will support a major expansion of manufacturing capacity for the US Navy and allied customers. Raytheon described the award as part of the Department of War’s wider “Arsenal of Freedom” effort to increase production of high-demand weapons.
Tomahawk is a long-range, subsonic precision-strike cruise missile used primarily to attack targets on land from substantial stand-off distances. In US naval service it can be launched from surface warships and submarines, giving commanders the ability to strike fixed and other designated targets hundreds of miles from the launch platform without placing crewed aircraft directly over the target area. Newer versions of the weapon have also expanded the missile’s targeting and maritime strike capabilities.
Raytheon President Phil Jasper said, as quoted in a news update: “Tomahawk is the Navy’s most important strike weapon, able to target hostile forces hundreds of miles away without ever risking the lives of our sailors.”
He added: “We are making significant investments in our workforce, technology, supply chain and facilities to dramatically boost production capacity and meet surging demand.”
The scale of the planned production increase is substantial. RTX said the new contract supports an annual manufacturing rate exceeding 1,000 Tomahawks, together with associated support. The company did not state that production is already running at that level, instead describing the figure as the target of the multi-year production ramp.
RTX has already been increasing deliveries. According to the company, Raytheon delivered three times as many Tomahawk missiles during the first half of 2026 as it did during the equivalent six months of 2025. The seven-year arrangement is intended to provide greater certainty to the manufacturer and its supply chain as production expands further.
Hundreds of small and medium-sized suppliers across the United States are expected to contribute to the programme. Long-term contracting can allow manufacturers further down the weapons supply chain to invest in machinery, staff and production capacity with greater confidence than under smaller annual orders, particularly where specialist components can otherwise become bottlenecks as final assembly rates increase.
Tomahawk has been in US service for decades and has been repeatedly used in combat for long-range conventional strikes. The weapon has undergone successive upgrades rather than being replaced outright, with later variants introducing changes to communications, targeting and mission flexibility while retaining the basic role of delivering precision effects at extended range.

articles.title: Iran and Oman discuss temporary Hormuz corridor
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran and Oman discuss temporary Hormuz corridor as impasse with US drags on
Iran said it had restarted talks with neighbor Oman to manage the Strait of Hormuz as it faces heightened economic pressure from US President Donald Trump in the wider conflict.
Iran and Oman have been in on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the strategic waterway, which handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February. Most shipping has been shut down since then.
The two countries said on Tuesday that they discussed "a joint temporary navigational corridor" through the strait and agreed to clear it of mines.
Trump said all mines in the strait had been cleared, repeating comments that he has previously made. Though active hostilities between the U.S. and Iran have largely subsided, diplomatic efforts to reach a peace deal have stalled and passage through the waterway remains perilous.
An oil tanker was struck on Tuesday by an unidentified projectile and disabled about 9 nautical miles (17 km) northeast of Oman's Ash Shishah, which lies at the entrance to the strait, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said.
Separately, the U.S. Secret Service said on Tuesday that it was aware of a video broadcast by Iranian state television discussing a potential plot to assassinate Trump's youngest son, Barron.
A three-minute video broadcast by Iranian state TV discussed a potential plot to assassinate Barron Trump, 20, claiming that he was being monitored and alleging that a $10 million bounty had been offered for his killing. '
SANCTIONS
Despite the ongoing tensions, the U.S. is beginning to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized amid tensions with Iran, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will initially operate below full capacity. In an effort to hobble Iran's economy, the United States earlier this week threatened to punish countries that continue to do business with Iran, but said it would not impose penalties immediately.
Oil prices fell for a second day as traders brushed off the impact of the U.S. sanctions, while Iran denounced the U.S. effort to isolate its economy as an act of "gross lawlessness", expressing confidence that many countries would not join the pressure campaign
U.S. public approval of the war has fallen to its lowest level since the conflict's early days, and Trump's popularity is likewise at a record low ahead of congressional elections in November, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
Thousands of people have died in the conflict, most of them in Iran and Lebanon, while the U.S. and Israel have degraded much of Iran's conventional military capacity. The exact state of its nuclear program, which the U.S. and Israel aim to dismantle, remains unknown.

articles.title: Forty-seven of Russia’s 50 top universities are advertising Defense Ministry contracts to students, investigation finds
articles.body:
Forty-seven of Russia’s 50 top universities are advertising Defense Ministry contracts to students, investigation finds
Forty-seven of Russia’s 50 top universities have urged students to sign contracts with the Defense Ministry, according to a study by the independent Russian news outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe.
The journalists relied on RAEX’s 2026 ranking of Russia’s 50 best universities. They analyzed posts on the schools’ own websites and social media accounts, information from students, and data published in various media outlets.
Novaya Gazeta Europe found that 44 of the universities advertise contract military service directly on their websites and social media accounts. Most of these ads promote enlistment in the Unmanned Systems Forces. At the Higher School of Economics, the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), and the Moscow Aviation Institute, meanwhile, students are urged to join the BARS-Moscow volunteer unit, whose duties include countering drones.
Twelve universities held special recruitment events touting the benefits of serving in the Unmanned Systems Forces. Three universities — Bauman Moscow State Technical University, the Moscow Engineering Physics Institute, and the Gubkin Russian State University of Oil and Gas — introduced dedicated classes on drones. Separately, 32 of the 50 leading Russian universities now offer educational programs related to drone development or operation.
Reports that students were being recruited to sign contracts with the Defense Ministry and sent to fight in Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine first surfaced in late 2025. Among other tactics, students are lured with extra payments from their universities and threatened with being denied the chance to retake failed exams.
The independent Russian political newsletter Faridaily said that Russian Science and Higher Education Minister Valery Falkov told the heads of the country’s largest universities in early 2026 that at least 2% of students must sign contracts with the Defense Ministry. According to the investigative outlet iStories, the Defense Ministry plans to recruit 78,800 people into the Unmanned Systems Forces by the end of 2026, with 58,000 of them to be drawn from students, graduates of drone operation courses, former service members of aviation units, and “female citizens” with relevant training.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Bail set for ex-Zelensky aide accused of money laundering
articles.body:
Bail set for ex-Zelensky aide accused of money laundering
Ukraine’s top anti-corruption court has set bail for the former deputy head of Vladimir Zelensky’s office, Irina Mudraya, at under $450,000 – less than one-seventh of the amount requested by prosecutors. She is suspected of channeling illicit funds into a bail payment for a defendant in a separate corruption case.
The High Anti-Corruption Court ruled on Tuesday that Mudraya must remain in Kiev and comply with any summons even if she posts bail, which she said she intends to do with the assistance of unnamed sponsors.
Zelensky fired Mudraya last week after she was formally accused of laundering about $3.3 million in cash to pay bail for former Energy Minister Herman Galushchenko. The latter had previously been implicated in an alleged $100 million kickback scheme blamed on Timur Mindich, a longtime associate of the Ukrainian leader.
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), two agencies established under Western pressure to tackle government graft, accused Mudraya of pressuring financial-monitoring officials to overlook suspicious transfers through Sense Bank. The lender was formerly the Ukrainian branch of Russia’s Alfa Bank before being nationalized by Kiev in 2023.
Surveillance recordings previously leaked to Ukrainian media suggested that Mindich’s group was interested in placing loyal figures on Sense Bank’s cabinet-appointed supervisory board. Ukrainian media dubbed Mindich “Zelensky’s bagman” amid suspicions that he was merely a frontman for corruption at the highest levels of government.
Mudraya trained as a lawyer specializing in banking and worked for several major clients in the sector before becoming a deputy justice minister in 2022. She moved to Zelensky’s office in 2024, ostensibly to contribute to Kiev’s efforts to obtain war reparations from Russia.
The former Zelensky aide has also been accused of participating in criminal schemes intended to expropriate real estate in Kiev worth some $16.75 million by illegally altering government records and pressuring judges to deny the legitimate owners legal recourse.
NABU and SAPO presented extensive records of conversations reportedly involving Mudraya and other suspects. The exchanges were allegedly recorded by former lawmaker and banker Maksim Mikitas.
Ukrainian media have speculated that Mikitas agreed to participate in the sting operation in return for leniency in other criminal cases being investigated by the two agencies.
During the bail hearings, Mudraya blamed a provocateur, apparently referring to Mikitas, for abusing her trust in order to produce incriminating recordings. She suggested that references to her alleged involvement in corruption were false but did not explain why she had failed to challenge the statements at the time.
Her defense team called several character witnesses, including Jonathan Markovitch, the chief rabbi of Kiev. He told the court that he knew Mudraya as a trustworthy member of the Jewish community and did not consider her a flight risk.
Mindich fled to Israel in November 2025, reportedly hours before he was due to be arrested. One of his key associates, Aleksandr Zukerman, also left for Israel. Both suspects hold Israeli citizenship.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian electronic warfare systems in Luhansk and Crimea, as well as depots in Zaporizhzhia Oblast
articles.body:
Ukraine hits Russian electronic warfare systems in Luhansk and Crimea, as well as depots in Zaporizhzhia Oblast
Ukraine's defence forces struck Russian electronic warfare systems in occupied Luhansk and in the village of Myrnyi in Crimea on 24 August and on the night of 24-25 August, as well as fuel, ammunition and logistics depots in Berdiansk and Prymorsk in Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Quote: "A specialised Peresvet-M electronic warfare system was struck in Luhansk.
A Starlink satellite communications jamming station was also struck in Myrnyi (temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea)."
Details: In Berdiansk, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine's defence forces struck a Russian fuel, lubricants and ammunition depot, while in Prymorsk, logistics depots belonging to one of the Russian units were hit.
In addition, data analysis has confirmed the damage to a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet at the Millerovo airfield in Russia's Rostov Oblast on 24 August.
The extent of the damage inflicted on Russian forces is being assessed.
Background: Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) reported that on the night of 23-24 August they struck Russian logistics centres belonging to Ozon marketplace, a Russian multirole MiG-29 fighter jet and dozens of other targets in Russia and in the temporarily occupied territories.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine receives 'a few' Patriot missiles, more needed
articles.body:
Following the recent summits of the NB8 and the Coalition of the Willing, Ukraine received "a few" Patriot missiles, AIM missiles, as well as confirmation regarding several Crotale air defense systems and missiles for them, reported President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"To be honest, a few Patriot missiles also arrived. How many, I cannot say, but a few. We need more," Zelenskyy said at a press conference with President of Estonia Alar Karis in Kyiv on Tuesday.
"We received confirmation – I won’t say from which country – of several Crotale air defense systems and missiles for them. And we also received Aim missiles. These are very important missiles for us. We use them to shoot down enemy missiles," the head of state added.
He also reported that over recent days, Ukraine received defense packages from Lithuania and Finland, confirmation regarding funding of EUR 9 billion for 2027 from Norway, and in addition, possible assistance from Sweden for the development of the Frejya office.
Zelenskyy also informed that Ukraine received several packages to support its regions, in particular, Mykolaiv and Zhytomyr regions. There are also support packages for veteran policy from Germany and Belgium, and Ukraine signed a drone deal with Norway.
"Germany separately supported Ukraine with an energy package. Sweden is providing a serious financial package to fund the production of Ukrainian drones. We are grateful for this," Zelenskyy summarized.

articles.title: CIA director Ratcliffe visits Moscow, US media reports
articles.body:
CIA director Ratcliffe visits Moscow, US media reports
CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Russia to attend meetings in Moscow on Tuesday, according to two US media outlets, in what is believed to be Ratcliffe's first known trip to Russia since taking over as US spy chief. The reported visit comes as US-brokered talks aimed at ending the Ukraine war have stalled.
US CIA Director John Ratcliffe travelled to Russia to attended meetings in Moscow on Tuesday, US media outlets reported citing unnamed sources.
CBS News and Axios both reported the visit by President Donald Trump's former director of national intelligence who now runs the nation's spy agency.
The outlets did not say who Ratcliffe was meeting with or what the talks are expected to cover.
CBS News said it was Ratcliffe's first known visit to Russia as CIA chief.
There was no immediate comment from the CIA or the White House. Data from Flightradar earlier showed a US military C-17 traveling from the US to Latvia and then Moscow.
Ratcliffe's reported visit comes as US-brokered talks aimed at ending Russia's invasion of Ukraine have stalled. But Moscow earlier this month freed a former US Marine detained since 2022 amid concerns about his health.
Read moreRussia frees ailing ex-US marine after four years in prison on disputed charges
The Iran war is also a live issue between Washington and and Tehran's ally Moscow.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Low-Cost Patriot PAC-3 ACE Missile Gets Simplified Motor and Seeker
articles.body:
The low-cost PAC-3 ACE missile, introduced by Lockheed Martin, features simplified components, particularly the motor and seeker.
Janes reported on this.
The main differences are a simplified seeker, the elimination of kinetic interception, and a simpler rocket motor.
In the standard PAC-3 MSE, these components are more complex and therefore more expensive, as the missile was designed to intercept modern ballistic missiles.
The missile was unveiled at the 2026 Farnborough International Airshow in the United Kingdom.
According to Lockheed Martin Vice President Jason Reynolds, the company aims to reduce the cost of the PAC-3 ACE to less than half that of the PAC-3 MSE.
To do so, engineers simplified several missile components. In particular, it will feature a simplified seeker system compared with the PAC-3 MSE. Lockheed Martin did not specify what type of seeker it will use.
The new missile will also omit the Attitude Control Motors (ACMs) used on the PAC-3 MSE. The company also simplified the missile’s midsection.
Another change will be the propulsion system. The PAC-3 ACE will use a single-mode solid-fuel rocket motor instead of the dual-pulse motor used by the PAC-3 MSE. Lockheed Martin is also considering the use of cheaper rocket motor casings.
A key difference will be the warhead. Instead of the hit-to-kill approach, which destroys the target through direct kinetic impact, the PAC-3 ACE will feature a blast-fragmentation warhead.
According to Reynolds, such a warhead reduces the need for terminal trajectory-correction systems, particularly ACMs or thrust-vector control systems.
At the same time, the PAC-3 ACE will retain the PAC-3 software used in the PAC-3 MSE. Lockheed Martin says the new missile is designed to counter aerodynamic targets, cruise missiles, and short-range ballistic missiles.
Militarnyi previously reported that the first flight test of the new low-cost PAC-3 ACE interceptor was expected in 18 months, with serial production set to begin “within a few years.”

articles.title: ‘Heat and shackles’: Russian soldiers freed from terrorist captivity in Mali talk to RT
articles.body:
‘Heat and shackles’: Russian soldiers freed from terrorist captivity in Mali talk to RT
Two Russian soldiers who spent more than two years in terrorist captivity in Mali have described to RT the extreme heat, constant shackling, poor food, and barely drinkable water they endured at the hands of Islamist militants.
Aleksandr Efremov and Vasily Nagalev spoke exclusively to RT’s Daria Vaganova after being brought to Libya on their way home to Russia.
The servicemen were captured in 2024 during the battle of Tinzaouaten near the Algerian border, when militants from the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) and Al-Qaeda-linked JNIM ambushed a Malian military convoy supported by Russia’s Wagner Group. The Malian and Wagner forces were heavily outnumbered in the fighting.
Efremov and Nagalev spent a total of 755 days in captivity, isolated from civilization and keeping track of time by counting sunrises and sunsets. They said the reality of captivity was nothing like what is typically portrayed in films.
“In movies, you can usually escape, but here there’s nowhere to run because there’s nothing but Sahara everywhere,” Aleksandr said, describing their ordeal as essentially “Sahara and chains.”
The soldiers said their legs were constantly shackled as they endured extreme heat and survived on poor food and barely drinkable water. After about a year, hope of being rescued began to fade.
“There was hope for about the first year, but by the second year, it didn’t matter anymore whether we’d be released or not,” Aleksandr recalled. “There were moments so tense that we practically begged to be shot.”
Their release was secured through negotiations involving the Russian Defense Ministry’s Africa Corps and the Malian General Staff, mediated by forces of the Libyan National Army led by General Saddam Haftar.
A Russian medical specialist treating the men after their release said the food they had received was “extremely detrimental to their bodies,” while they had been “practically drinking from a puddle.”
“They have problems with their intestines, liver, and other organs,” he said, adding that doctors were “gradually restoring them” to health. Both men are currently in “stable and satisfactory” condition and could return to Russia within “a week or two” once their condition has fully stabilized.
Efremov and Nagalev told RT they intend to continue serving in the Russian military after recovering and plan to join Moscow’s military operation against Kiev.
The Sahel has been plagued by militant violence for more than a decade, with groups linked to Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS), Al-Qaeda, and Boko Haram carrying out attacks across Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and neighboring countries. Moscow has repeatedly accused foreign powers, including Ukraine, of seeking to destabilize the region and undermine local nations’ ties with Russia by assisting extremist groups.
The freed soldiers said their captors appeared to be receiving substantial outside support.
“They certainly receive money because they have everything,” Vasily said.
“They have money, equipment, weapons. They have it all. And in large quantities,” Aleksandr added.
The Wagner Group, with which the two men previously served, has since ended its operations in Mali, with Russia’s Africa Corps taking over its role in supporting Sahel governments in their fight against militants and extremists.
In mid-July, Malian and Russian forces recaptured the strategic northern town of Anefis from FLA and JNIM after more than a week of intense fighting. In mid-August, Russian troops also helped the Malian military repel a large-scale attack on an army base in the central city of San.

articles.title: For first time, Ukraine is tendering ground robots to ministry-set specifications and no maker can take more than half of any class
articles.body:
Ukraine's ground robots ran more than 100,000 missions in the first eight months of 2026. The Defense Procurement Agency will now buy logistics and strike ground robotic complexes according to specifications set by the Defense Ministry, rather than approving models one at a time, the ministry announced.
The mechanism is three days old. The agency applied the same structure to fiber-optic FPV drones on 22 August—classes, multiple lots each, no supplier above half a class. Ukraine is standardizing how it buys entire weapons categories, one category at a time.
The rules sort makers by class
Complexes will be divided into classes by operating range and payload, with four to five lots per class. No single manufacturer may take more than half the order within one class.
Suppliers must meet the technical specifications and hold at least one codified ground robotic complex. The procurement runs in a closed environment under defense security requirements.
"A tender is one of the best instruments for this, because we can buy more equipment for the same money and minimize the risk of supply disruptions by splitting the order among different manufacturers," Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik said.
Mission volume keeps climbing
Monthly figures of ground robot missions logged in the DELTA combat system rose almost without interruption: 7,511 in January, 11,028 in April, 19,969 in July. Units recorded another 15,729 between 1 and 20 August, about 790 a day compared with roughly 640 a day in July, The Defense Post reported.
Ukraine has contracted more than 22,000 ground robots since January, nearly double the total for all of 2025. The number of units operating them grew from 117 at the end of 2025 to 230 by mid-2026.
A commander disputes the evacuation case
The ministry lists casualty evacuation as one of the tender's purposes. A frontline officer challenged that three days ago.
Tetiana Chornovol, who commands an anti-tank guided missile platoon, said ground robots are too slow for evacuation and often easy targets for Russian drones, arguing brigades need staffed evacuation teams and small light-armored vehicles instead.

articles.title: Russia’s attack drones now jam the cheap interceptors sent to kill them
articles.body:
Ukraine's cheap interceptor drones have been knocking Russia's nightly attackers out of the sky, so Russia has now bolted a jammer onto some of its own drones to blind them, according to Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine's President on defense technology. He examined the system, found in drone wreckage, and mapped how it strikes back at the interceptor sent to hunt it.
Russia batters Ukrainian cities with long-range drones most nights, and Ukraine has leaned on a cheap shield—drones costing a few thousand dollars—instead of burning through far pricier missiles. Anything that dulls that shield pushes the cost of defending the sky back up.
A jammer that waits for the interceptor
The unit rides on a Geran, Russia's version of the Iranian Shahed one-way drone. It listens for the video signal an approaching Ukrainian interceptor beams back to its pilot. Its receiver reads the interceptor's working frequency, then orders a transmitter to bury that same channel in noise, Beskrestnov found.
How Ukraine uses AI to guide long-range drone strikes through electronic warfare and deep into Russian-controlled rear areas
By his first estimate, the jammer's signal runs about five times stronger than the interceptor's video link—enough to wipe the picture and any chance of steering the drone onto its target.
Seconds decide it
In Beskrestnov's account, the system detected a test transmitter and switched on jamming after about three seconds, and the feed cut out. The device stays nearly idle until a hunter comes close, then jumps to full power to smother the signal. It targets the ordinary analog video band around 5.8 gigahertz that many cheap interceptors still use.
Possible answers, include interceptors with terminal-guidance homing for the final stretch of flight, digital communication links, or transmitters set to non-standard frequencies.
“Two targets and ammo with one drone”: How a Ukrainian drone crew hunts Russian transport behind the front line
An old problem for Russia's drones
Russia has tried again and again to keep its one-way drones alive against Ukraine's defenses, including wiring jammers into some Shaheds earlier this year. Spending weight and power to protect a drone from a far cheaper interceptor shows how well those cheap drones work.
